en: In the fifty-fourth fascicle of the *Shi Dunlun Jizhuan Lunben* (The Collected Explanations of the Treatise by Shi Dunlun),

within the section on the distinctions of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), there are first five chapters presented in general, followed by a detailed explanation. This is the explanation of "abiding" (*sthiti*).
Zhongjing Buke said:
"The various consciousnesses of the desire realm for the most part grasp at the external five sensory objects; they are established upon form and name."
The various consciousnesses of the form realm dwell together with their attachment to the five internal aggregates.
The mental consciousness of the formless realm dwells solely within the names of those four aggregates.
Ji says:
Regarding the fact that the desire realm (kāmadhātu) refers exclusively to external objects:
this is because, due to the habituation to sensual desires, one is largely attached to external objects;
furthermore, although craving also arises toward the internal body, one remains settled therein.
Because birth occurs through the womb, eggs, and so forth, it is not a supreme abiding;
now, we discuss it according to what is supreme.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one speaks only of the internal body.
Because they are born by transformation (*upapāduka*), they do not practice desire.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one speaks only of the name produced by the karma of abiding;
one does not speak of matter transformed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is the intended meaning of this passage.
As for the term "clinging" (*upādāna*) mentioned here,
it refers to the grasping of objects that are not appropriated (*anupātta*).
Because names are not what is appropriated.
Regarding this, the *Buzhique* (Supplement) states:
First, regarding the gate of experiencing objects within the present life:
at the time when the causes manifest, consciousness is defiled by attachment to the five sensory objects of the present.
Second, regarding the gate of birth, aging, and so forth within future lives:
When the subsequent fruit ripens, consciousness is defiled by the increase of various afflictions such as birth, aging, and death.
Ji (基) states:
"The former is the defilement of affliction."
The latter is the defilement of birth;
furthermore, the latter is the defilement of karma.
Because of the defilement of karma, future birth and so forth become defiled.
Regarding the "basis" (*āśraya*),
Buke (Supplement) says:
"This means that the six consciousnesses follow their respective faculties."
The names differ,
just as fire, depending on its fuel, has various distinct names while abiding therein.
First, the chapter is cited as the question;
second, the explanation;
third, the conclusion after the explanation has been completed.
Within the explanation, there are again two parts.
First, the enumeration is presented and the meaning of "abiding" is briefly explained by citing a sūtra.
Second, from the passage beginning with "Thus it has already been revealed... down to "...from this point onward," etc.
The Master of the Treatise explains this extensively.
Within the preceding section,
if one were to supplement it, it would say:
The meaning of the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) is analyzed through four gates.
First, the origin of the teaching is clarified:
non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to consciousness as the self (*ātman*) and the other four aggregates (*skandha*) as the locus where that self dwells.
The Buddha refuted this attachment and addressed them, saying:
"Form, feeling, perception, and formations are that in which consciousness dwells, but they are not the self.
For this reason, the Blessed One taught the meaning of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Second, the definition of the essence: the four contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) constitute the essence of the stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
Because these contaminated aggregates can give rise to lustful defilement and cause consciousness to dwell with pleasure, they are established as the stations of consciousness.
Untainted feeling (*anāsravā vedanā*) and so forth are not objects that give rise to craving.
Consciousness accompanied by outflows (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) does not abide in consciousness itself; thus, consciousness is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Non-Buddhists merely cling to the four aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), as the dwelling place of the self.
In contrast to that, the four aggregates are established as the stations of consciousness;
therefore, consciousness itself is not established as a station of consciousness.
Furthermore, because the four aggregates—form and the others—are either defiled by nature or possess a strong capacity to produce defilement, they are established as stations of consciousness.
The nature of consciousness is not defiled; defilement alone cannot establish the abiding of consciousness.
Third, the explanation of the name:
"discerning" (vijñapti) is the meaning of consciousness (vijñāna).
"Delightful abiding" (sukhavihāra) signifies the sense of dwelling.
"Four" (catvāri) is a numerical designation;
thus, this name is derived from the number applied to the meaning.
These are called the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Fourth, the distinction between the Great and Small [Vehicles] is elucidated.
According to the Sarvāstivāda, "abiding" (*sthiti*) is understood as being supported by a basis (*āśraya*).

This means that when contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) relies upon those four aggregates (*skandha*)—form and the others—which arise simultaneously with it, this is called its "abode" (*sthiti*).
It is not the case that consciousness apprehending an object is what is termed an "abode of consciousness.
Therefore, that treatise states: "One's own consciousness abides in one's own aggregates."
It does not differ in realm, nor in level, nor in body,
because two [minds] are non-concurrent in a single moment.
The consciousness-abiding does not regard its own nature as its own nature.
When untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) or consciousness belonging to another realm manifests,
although the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) of one's own level lack a specific consciousness as their support,
they nevertheless obtain the intermediate causal conditions for the characteristic of being a "dwelling of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
Thus, one's own consciousness does not arise;
if it were to arise later, it would merely follow along with that [external object].
Furthermore, he refutes alternative theories, saying:
Some say that it is incorrect to claim that the aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings are called "stations of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
Rather, the meaning of "station of consciousness" refers to the sense of being supported by formations (*saṃskāra*) and being associated with conditions.
According to this reasoning, the text here quotes the opponent's position, omitting two characters.
It is not correct to say that there are aggregates not included among the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*) which are nevertheless called "stations of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
In our own school, "station" is understood as a basis for abiding;
aggregates not included among the category of sentient beings are not the support for consciousness.
Therefore, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Below, the meaning of "abiding" (*sthiti*) is explained through five points;
this specifically excludes non-sentient things (*asattva*), which are not established as stations of consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that the meaning of "abiding" (*vijñānasthiti*) refers to the sense of being a basis for the association with formations (*saṃskāra*).
As for "basis," internal form, sensation, and so forth serve as the basis for consciousness.
"Conduct" refers to the three aggregates, such as feeling, which share the same mode of activity and understanding as consciousness.
"Object-condition" refers to—
Feeling and the other [mental factors] share the same object of cognition as consciousness;
this is precisely the meaning of the fourth [characteristic], "concomitance" (saṃprayukta) with consciousness.
"Part" (bhāga) has the meaning of "cause" (hetu).
Internal matter and consciousness share a common basis of safety and peril, acting as a proximate efficient cause for one another;
feeling and the other [mental factors] act as associated co-existent causes for consciousness.
Therefore, they are called "parts" (bhāga).
By means of these five meanings, the "abiding" (āśraya) is established.
If one takes the aggregates that are non-sentient in number, they are also called stations of consciousness (vijñāna-sthiti);
this refers to abiding by way of objective conditions (ālambana).
This would contradict the meaning of our own school’s reliance on the principle of abiding;
the *Abhidharmakośa* also states that the aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings constitute the substance of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The preceding section concludes according to the Hīnayāna school.
Now, in the Mahāyāna, both the basis of reliance (*niśraya*) and the object of cognition (*ālambana*) are accepted;
it is not solely by way of reliance.
In this text, the statement that "the mental consciousness dwells following form" means it dwells in dependence upon it;
that "it takes form as its object" means it dwells by way of taking it as an object.
If one considers only dwelling in dependence, it relies solely upon the four aggregates of form and so forth within one's own continuum.
If it were to abide by taking conditions as its support, then it would abide in common with both self and other, as well as with insentient phenomena. Why is this so?
Because such is the logical necessity.
In general, "abode of consciousness" (vijñāna-sthiti) has the meaning of attachment.
What constitutes abiding through attachment?
It is that which causes consciousness to dwell with pleasure by means of an object stained by craving.
Therefore, consciousness-dwelling (*vijñāna-sthiti*) and object-dwelling (*ālambana-sthiti*) are called "dwelling.
Just as internal forms and so forth are established as consciousness-dwellings because they give rise to craving for objects and cause consciousness to dwell with pleasure,
so too external to one's own body— whether sentient or insentient things such as the five objects of desire— give rise to craving for objects and cause consciousness to dwell with pleasure.
Why are they not stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*)?
For this reason, both internal and external forms and so forth, which serve as the objects of consciousness, are all established as stations of consciousness;
yet the followers of the Hīnayāna claim that they are established as stations of consciousness only in relation to one's own body, while external forms and so forth are not.
The meaning of "abiding" (sthiti) would not be established.

Furthermore, sentient beings of the desire realm are mostly attached to external objects such as the five sensual pleasures; their mutual passion and defilement draw the consciousness and cause it to abide—this is precisely what constitutes a "station of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti).

To say that external objects—whether sentient or insentient, such as forms and so forth—give rise to craving and produce consciousness, yet consciousness does not establish its dwelling therein, is not logical.
Therefore, in the Mahāyāna, all contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) that take objects as their conditions are termed "dwelling" (*sthiti*).
The principle that "the meaning of being subsumed and abiding is exhaustive" is established.
Question:
If it is understood by taking "abiding" as the object-condition (*ālambana*), [how is this so?]
This means that consciousness of one lifetime takes dharmas of three lifetimes as its object;
or consciousness of one realm takes dharmas of three realms as its object;
or when tainted consciousness takes the untainted truths of Cessation and the Path as its objects.
Is it that all are established as stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*) based on their being objects of perception?
The explanation says:
because other [consciousnesses] take those past, future, and present contaminated (*sāsrava*) four aggregates as objects, they cause consciousness to dwell with pleasure therein.

Therefore, it is accepted that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) form and so forth of the three time periods, when considered in relation to the consciousness of a single time period, are all termed "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
Furthermore, when craving for a lower realm craves a higher stage, it draws consciousness toward dwelling in pleasure; thus, this too is established as an abode of consciousness.
The two truths of cessation and the path are not objects for craving;
although they are conditioned by consciousness,
they do not cause it to increase.
The stations of consciousness are not established.
Question:
Consciousness is drawn forth by craving.
Does it cause them to abide simultaneously,
or do they induce one another through a sequence of before and after?
The commentary states:
This has two meanings.
First, there are tainted consciousnesses associated with craving that, by means of the simultaneous craving, draw and maintain the object before them.
This is exclusively an afflicted consciousness.
Alternatively, there may be craving that first defiles the preceding object and induces the subsequent consciousness;
in this case, the consciousness permeates all three natures.
It arises from the preceding greed.
Question:
How is it known that lower greed conditions the upper [realms] to draw forth consciousness so that it dwells in pleasure?
The commentary states:
As for the fifty-eighth [section], it says:
"These ten kinds of afflictions thus described..."
All [afflictions] mutually serve as objects for one another among all afflictions of oneself and others.
Furthermore, afflictions of a lower stage can take as their objects both the afflictions and the objective bases of a higher stage.
Furthermore, the sixty-second [treatise] states:
"If one is born in a lower stage and gives rise to craving for a higher stage, yet has not attained detachment from desire and possesses an indeterminate mind, this is bound to the Desire Realm.
Being possessed by defilement, the defiled person thinks: 'I shall now realize the meditative attainment (samāpatti) arising from vast joy and bliss.'"
"If I were to attain realization, I would savor it;
furthermore, how might I be born in the higher realms, remaining eternal and unchanging?
Such craving is defiled.
This is based on the fact that the afflictions of craving take the "attainment of what is superior" as their object.
Question:
Among the eight consciousnesses, which consciousness first takes what as its object such that the four stations of consciousness (*catur-vijñāna-sthiti*) are explained?
The commentary states:
If one intends to encompass all phenomena exhaustively, one takes all eight consciousnesses;
if one proceeds according to what is most manifest in their characteristics, one takes only the six consciousnesses.
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the sūtra," there are three brief explanations cited here based on the subsequent text.
First is called the causal condition for the abiding of consciousness;
second is called the limit of the abiding of consciousness;
third is called the cessation of the causal conditions for the abiding of consciousness.
What is now called "the four" refers to the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
As for the phrase "relying on grasping" (*upādāna*), it means...
This means that both manifest greed and its seeds constitute the essence of grasping (*upādāna*).
Since these are the four bases for the abiding of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the locus of the four conditions,
it is said that [consciousness] "depends on grasping."
Because one abides by depending on these appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), and because they serve as the condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*) to cause it to abide,
it is said that "consciousness dwells following form and takes form as its object.
The detailed explanation is as in the Sūtra.
This is the first causal condition for the abiding of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

As for the statement, "I shall never say that this consciousness goes to the east, nor even to the four intermediate directions," this clarifies the limits of the causal conditions for the abiding of consciousness.
This is the second gate.

It clarifies that consciousness, following the four aggregates throughout the duration of a single lifetime, does not depart from those four aggregates and cannot proceed to the four cardinal or four intermediate directions;
this is precisely what is termed the "limit of the abode of consciousness."

Furthermore, apart from the four stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) which exist outside of both manifest greed and its latent tendencies (anuśaya), there are none that serve as causes and conditions; these are precisely the limits of the causes and conditions for the stations of consciousness.
However, I speak only of those within the present life who have reached even the state of coolness and purity.
This is the third [point], clarifying that both the abodes of consciousness and their causal conditions are completely stilled.
"One who must be free from desire" refers to being free from the causal conditions for the abodes of consciousness.
This refers to being free from the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
It is the cessation of causes and conditions.
As for the phrase "free from shadows": [it means]...
Because feeling arises from the tree of consciousness, it is said that feeling is its shadow.
At that time, when there is no longer existence, one is eternally free from the shadow;
because all tainted consciousness has been exhausted, there is quiescent extinction.
This clarifies that consciousness abides in tranquility.
Next, there are three phrases that clarify the different names for untainted consciousness at its preceding and succeeding stages:
that of the learner (*śaikṣa*) is called "tranquility."
The state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is called "cooling" (*śītala*);
the cessation without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirodha*) is called "purity" (*viśuddhi*).
Tai says:
Various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintain that after death the self goes to the east, west, and so forth;
this [view] is now refuted.
As the treatise below states: "The causes and conditions for the abiding of consciousness have two kinds of limits."
This means that in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is coming and going;
in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), consciousness has neither coming nor going.
Therefore, it is not said that [consciousness] goes toward the four intermediate directions.
Therefore, one should know that these are two kinds of limits;
because the stations of consciousness do not exist apart from the three realms,
the meaning of "abiding" is said to be exhaustive.
Therefore it is called the "limit.
Master Ji says:
as stated in the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (18), it is like this: [text follows].
It abides in accordance with form;
that is to say, because it is the basis for what is appropriated.
It abides by taking form as its object.
"Grasping at objects" means because of seizing upon objective spheres.
"Abiding in dependence on form" means because of the presence of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
This refers precisely to the basis for grasping;
that is, there are four stations,
namely, from form up to volitional formations.
The fourth is the fruit of consciousness,
because it is the object of consciousness.
Regarding "depending on grasping":
This refers to grasping (*upādāna*) based on this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The essence of grasping consists of the various afflictions (*kleśa*).

Therefore, the subsequent passage explains that the essence of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the stations of causal conditions (*hetupratyayasthiti*) consists of the four causal conditions, such as form (*rūpa*), which are precisely the greed and other afflictions that arise from them.
Regarding "the entities of the afflictions," this refers to the actual manifestation of the various delusions;
"belonging to those afflictions" refers to their seeds.
As for the term "causal condition":
This refers to the causes and conditions by which consciousness dwells within form and so forth;
it explains the reason why consciousness dwells within these four, beginning with form.
Because it takes this grasping as its basis,
it is called the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As the Tripiṭaka Master says:
Because one takes them as objects of focus by means of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*),
consciousness is made to abide upon form and so forth, and so on at length.
Now, it is said that these four are the "bases" (*āśraya*) from which consciousness proceeds toward grasping (*upādāna*).
Using this as the object of focus (ālambana),
one causes consciousness to abide therein;
the term "object" contains two meanings.
If it is taken in the sense of being an object of cognition (*ālambana*),
it applies to both the internal and the external;
if it is taken in the sense of being an objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), it likewise applies to both.
Regarding the statement, "The meaning of the text is not like the conditions of the scriptural sources;
within the present life, one will certainly be free from the shadow of desire," the commentary says:
Because the noble disciple practices and cultivates [this] extensively,
he is able to sever the four bodily fetters in this very life.
These four bodily fetters arise solely from the conceptualization of the mental ground.
Therefore, they are abandoned at the time of the path of seeing.
These four types of desire consist of the longing for a future body and so forth.
"Reflection" refers to sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth;
the following provides a detailed explanation.
First, the preceding summary is concluded and the subsequent detailed exposition is introduced;
thereafter, the actual explanation follows.
Within that explanation:
First, the opening explanation of the obstacles;
second, clarifying the reasons for establishing or rejecting the position that consciousness is not established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Within the first section, there are further two parts.
First, the three meanings are opened up;
second, they are distinguished according to the chapters.
That is to say, within this sutra, there is one chapter that briefly reveals the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the characteristics of their causal conditions.
This refers back to the preceding sutra passage stating that there are four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) which are taken as objects of focus to cause consciousness to abide, and so forth.
The phrase "the two types of limits regarding the causes and conditions for the abiding of consciousness" opens the second chapter.
He then cites the preceding sutra, up to the passage: "I never say that this consciousness dwells in the eastern direction, nor even in the four intermediate directions.
The statement, "The causes and conditions for the dwelling of consciousness are twofold tranquility," opens the third chapter.
He then cites the preceding sutra: "I have spoken only of that which, within this very life, is necessarily free from desire, shadowless, extinguished, tranquil, cool, and pure.
Below this, he provides an explanation in three sections.
This constitutes three sections.
Within the first chapter,
there is first the exposition and finally the conclusion.
The explanation consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the causal conditions;
second, the explanation of the stations of consciousness.
In the explanation of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda),
there is first a brief summary,
followed by a detailed exposition.
"One should know that herein, up to the phrase 'because there is an object of perception,' this is the brief explanation.
Thus says Buke (Supplementer).
"Those things which are afflictions" refers to the manifest occurrence of afflictions.
"Those that belong to those afflictions" [refers to the factors associated with them].
The seeds of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
which produce subsequent afflictions through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of those afflictions,
are said to belong to the afflictions.
It is called "that which relies on grasping.
One should know that these two are also termed "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*), as previously cited in the sūtra.
The manifest afflictions and their seeds are the objective supports (*ālambana*) for the four stations of consciousness;
therefore, they are also called "objective supports.
As for the phrase "because of having the nature of an objective support":
Thus, the phenomena of the various afflictions that previously appeared are of the nature of objective referential cognition;
this is what is meant by "the nature of objective referential cognition. As for the statement, "because there is an object of reference":
These seeds of affliction are capable of producing the objective phenomena (ālambana-dharma) of manifest afflictions.
Ji states:
"In this context, the seeds of the formations are all of the nature of grasping (upādāna)."
If, as in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, "grasping" (*upādāna*) is defined solely as the essence of desire and lust (*kāmarāga*),
then "predominance" (*adhipatya*) refers here to its application to all afflictions (*kleśa*) according to their actual meaning.
Furthermore, the "basis" consists of the four objects;
one should know that herein it is also termed the "object-condition" (ālambana).
Because it is that which is taken as an object and because there is that which possesses an object,
both the manifest and the seeds are termed "objects" (ālambana).
The seeds function precisely as conditions for others.
That which manifests and is capable of having an object is therefore called an "object" (ālambana).
As for the nature of being an object:
This is precisely the seed.
That which possesses an object of perception is the manifest activity.
In the detailed explanation below,
first the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are explained,
and subsequently the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are explained.
Regarding the preceding section:
first, it clarifies that such craving serves as the condition for affliction.
Regarding "the objects grasped by the destinies":
through the craving for those [objects], one is led by various afflictions toward the self-referential domains of the destinies.
Next, the four fetters (*saṃyojana*) are explained as the conditions for the production of karma.
Buque states: "The old name for these was the 'four bonds' (*bandhana*)."
These are now called the four fetters (*saṃyojana*).
However, there is a difference between this and the Abhidharma;
for the latter states that the fetter of greed (*rāga-bandhana*) pervades the three realms and is abandoned through all six or five categories of abandonment.
At present, we consider only the mental level (*manobhūmi*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This distinguishes between the two types of abandonment: greed and hatred arise from conceptualization (*vikalpita*), while their bondage extends across all six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*).
Now, we take only those two types of hatred arising from discrimination on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*) that are of the nature to be abandoned [by the path of seeing].
As for the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the grasping at what is real (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), these also pertain to all three realms;
however, here too we take only those arising from discrimination in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) which are of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*).
Because the non-discrimination of the upper realms is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
Thus, these four fetters, acting as conditions that give rise to karma, are called the "objects of focus" (*ālambana-vastu*);
if karma is the condition for maturation (*vipāka-pratyaya*), it is likewise called an "object of focus."
Furthermore, because the four bonds (catvāro granthāḥ) serve as conditions for the substance of karma,
they are called "the objects conditioned by [karma]. Ji says:
The very substance of karma is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of its fruit;
because it is one with the object and serves as the condition for the fruit,
these four fetters (saṃyojana) act as the conditions for karma.
Because they are able to give rise to karma,
they are called "objects of focus" (*ālambana-vastu*).
The four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*) have greed as their essence, just as they are defined in the *Abhidharma*.
Regarding the mention of "this text," here only four types are taken up;
these are the objects of craving. That [previous passage] was based on the subjective faculty of cognition.
This is based on their objects of perception (*ālambana*).
They arise solely from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and do not extend to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Hatred and the like are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and do not extend to the higher realms.
Therefore, the object-condition for craving extends throughout the three realms.
Next, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are explained;
for those two [cravings] are pursued by the latent dispositions.
Regarding the "establishment of the basis":
this refers to the seeds of greed and the four fetters.
These two latent tendencies (anuśaya) that give rise to the phenomena of affliction are called the "establishment of the basis."
The preceding section has concluded the identification of the causes and conditions for the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Below, the actual nature of the stations of consciousness is clarified.
As for those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained the antidote of weary detachment and still possess craving and delight:
This is because the antidote of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has not yet been cultivated.
As for the consciousness that is moistened by this [compassion], which is capable of grasping and fulfilling the future internal body:
it is because within the *ālayavijñāna* there exist the seeds of karma.
Because it is moistened by craving, it fully grasps the single consciousness of the future,
which abides within as the inferior retribution.
Regarding the phrase "by this, successively," etc.:
Afflictions give rise to karma;
karma, in turn, brings about retribution;
and retribution, in turn, gives rise to further delusion.
Delusion returns to initiate karma;
karma proceeds to draw forth retribution.
Hence it is said that they "revolve and turn."
Birth and death are without end.
Regarding the remaining causal conditions for abiding, they should be understood as previously explained,
such as the arising and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) discussed above.
"This is called a brief explanation of the characteristics of abiding and its causal conditions" is the conclusion.
From here below, the two limits are clarified.
Regarding the statement that "consciousness in the realm of form has coming and going, while consciousness in the formless realm has death and birth," the *Bùquē* (Supplement) says:
"The consciousness of the two lower realms is said to have coming and going because it relies upon matter for its transmission and maintenance."
It is not so for the formless realm.
It is simply stated that within this body, consciousness dies, and within another body, consciousness is born.
Ji says:
There are those with form and body, and those without form and body.
Being born in this place and dying in this very place clarifies that in the two lower realms there are four aggregates as stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
whereas in the upper realm of formlessness, there are only three aggregates as stations.
Furthermore, those with form possess the intermediate state (antarābhava),
whereas those without form do not have an intermediate state;
therefore, there is death and there is birth.
If that is so, how can it be said that these two abide until the end of their lifespan?
The former interpretation is superior.
Furthermore, regarding these two abodes up until the exhaustion of the lifespan:
the consciousness of coming and going and the consciousness of death and birth constitute the two.
This clarifies that the scope of the abode of consciousness extends to this limit.
Therefore, it is called the "limit" (*koṭi*).
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the growth, increase, and expansion of these two, it should be understood as previously stated:
it is due to the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Consciousness has coming and going, and it has death and birth.
Apart from this, there is no other causal condition that can be called the limit of conditions (*pratyaya-paryanta*).
This restates the two: consciousness that has coming and going, and consciousness that has death and birth.
The meaning of these two—namely, their growth, increase, and expansion—should be understood as previously explained.
Apart from what has been analyzed above, there are no others that are not causal conditions (*pratyaya*);
thus, the very term "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the limit of conditions.

From "Equalizing this" onwards, there is the double conclusion regarding the two limits. As for "if one were to further establish [them] otherwise," up to "even if one were to establish them in such a way": The meaning is as follows: if one were to establish the limit of the past by means of the future, or establish the limit of the future by means of the past; or if one were to establish the limit of the past by means of the present, or establish the limit of the present by means of the past; or if one were to establish the limit of the future by means of the present, or establish the limit of the present by means of the future—then, because these three times would each mutually encompass one another, they would all become identical. Because they would all become identical, there would be no distinction between the three times. Because there would be no distinction between the three times, one would fall into the error of asserting that the three times are eternal. Therefore, it is said: "If one were to further establish [them] otherwise. Furthermore, "up to even if one were to establish them in such a way" means: if one were to establish the limit of the past by means of both the future and the present, or establish the limit of the future by means of both the past and the present; or if one were to establish the limit of the past by means of both the future and the present, or establish the limit of the present by means of both the future and the past; or if one were to establish the limit of the future by means of both the past and the present, or establish the limit of the present by means of both the past and the future—then, because these three times would each mutually encompass one another, they would all become identical. Because they would all become identical, there would be no distinction between the three times. Because there would be no distinction between the three times, one would fall into the error of asserting that the three times are eternal. Therefore, it is said: "up to even if one were to establish them in such a way. This is the meaning.
This refutes divergent views. Buque says:
"If there were a distinct self, then the two types of limits previously established by me would follow."
Furthermore, regarding the establishment [of teachings],
one should know that there are three faults:
first, there are words without meaning.
Second, if another asks a question correctly and one does not know how to answer;
third, even if one answers falsely, one will later realize for oneself that it was a statement born of delusion.
Tai says: [as follows].
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also because of the absence of objects due to other reasons":
if it were like the consciousness of the *puruṣa* (self) as established by the non-Buddhists,
then since its objects do not exist, one would not know how to answer [the question of its cognition].
The above clarifies the deluded non-Buddhists;
furthermore, there are those with sharp faculties who are likewise confused, as clarified below, in their questioning.
From here below is the third section, clarifying the two types of tranquility (*śamatha*).
Within this, there are three parts.
The first clarifies the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and the abiding of consciousness in tranquility.
Second, explaining the distinctions in the superior benefits of the consciousnesses that can be countered and eliminated;
third, interpreting the meaning of the six phrases in the sutra.
Within the first [section], there are four parts.
First, clarifying the cessation of the causal conditions for the abiding of consciousness;
second, clarifying the cessation of the abiding of consciousness;
third, concluding with the cessation of the causal conditions.
The fourth is the cessation of the abodes of consciousness through the settling [of the mind]. Within this,
the first clarifies the cessation of the various matters of the afflictions.
Second, the explanation of the pacification of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Within the preceding section,
first, the formal thesis is established.
The second part provides the explanation,
from "If one who is wise" up to "is able to permanently sever and abandon.
Those of the Three Vehicles who are noble ones (ārya) are called "wise."
The ability to eliminate craving and attachment is called "permanent severance and detachment.

As for the statement that one can also permanently sever the four bodily fetters (*kāyabandhana*) and the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) that initiate karma— which are comprised within the various states of the afflictions (*kleśa*)—
this is due to the severance of craving and attachment.
The four fetters are eternally severed.
Why is this? [This is] an inquiry from an outsider.
Why is it that by severing the four bodily fetters of craving for the stations of consciousness, they are forever severed?
The answer below is: because householders, relying on the fetters of greed and hatred, initiate various karmic actions.
In summary:
"Because grasping at objects serves as the cause" means that by craving the five sensory objects, one is able to initiate karma.
Regarding the phrase "because it has the harming of sentient beings as its cause":
because one gives rise to hatred toward sentient beings, one is able to initiate karma.
If members of the monastic community rely on the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), [they likewise initiate karma].

This adherence to what is real consists of two fetters that incite karma: the adherence to precepts and observances, which is like craving for rebirth in heaven; and the adherence to what is real, which is like anger toward those who slander nirvāṇa.
In general, when one perceives through grasping at views that something is real,
asserting "only this is real and all else is not," is called the denial of nirvāṇa.

The general intent of the answer here is that the four fetters (*saṃyojana*) are likewise categorized as belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the mental level (*manobhūmi*), and those arising from discrimination (*vikalpaja*).
However, among these four fetters:
Craving is precisely the abiding of consciousness through attachment;
therefore, when craving is severed, the four bonds are also severed.
Question:
How is it known that the four bonds (*catvāraḥ saṃyojanāni*) are severed simultaneously with craving?
Therefore, the treatise answers: "It should be understood that the four bodily bonds arise solely from the conceptualization of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*)."

Since these four fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) share the same nature as craving (*tṛṣṇā*)— namely, that they are grasped by the mind and arise from mental discrimination—
the severing of craving eliminates the four fetters.
What doubt can there be regarding these two?
The preceding section has clarified the pacification of the mind’s afflictions;
the following clarifies the pacification of the seeds and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
From this point onward, through the extensive cultivation of superior remedies, one is able to permanently sever craving, the four bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*), and the two types of latent tendencies.
The preceding section has already clarified the cessation of the causal conditions for the stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
Regarding the phrase "by the abandonment of these,

up to their ultimate separation," this clarifies that because the causal conditions for the stations of consciousness are abandoned, the substance of the four stations of consciousness produced from those causes also ceases to continue.
Therefore, it is called "the consciousness abiding in tranquility.
As for the statement, "because the objects of focus do not continue in succession, [consciousness] does not abide therein," this means that the four types of objects do not persist.
The consciousness that takes contaminated phenomena as its object also does not abide securely;
this is because the causes and conditions for the third level of fetters below have been pacified through their antidote,
and because the consciousness that abides in the fourth level of fetters below will likewise be pacified in the future.

Furthermore, below the statement "the pure consciousness subsumed under the antidote is called 'dwelling nowhere,'" the superior distinctions of the victorious power of the remedial consciousness are clarified.
Below that, "dwelling nowhere" is explained by means of four meanings.
First, by way of non-arising:
because greed and the other afflictions are permanently severed,
it is called "non-arising."
Second, by having nothing further to accomplish;
third, by contentment;
fourth, by abiding securely.
Because they do not grow in this way,
the first fetter [is abandoned],
up to and including abiding.
This concludes the fourth section.
It is named "Ultimate Liberation" because it fully incorporates the five meanings— both general and specific— discussed previously.
Therefore, that untainted mind is called "ultimate liberation.
Furthermore, because one does not cling at all to a self or what belongs to a self regarding formations and so forth, one does not give rise to fear when form and the other aggregates perish.
Therefore, the untainted mind has already attained purity.
Furthermore, because that consciousness is eternally pure, it enters into quiescent extinction spontaneously and naturally, without depending on any other cause.
By means of the untainted (*anāsrava*), which is eternally pure and does not depend on other causes, one enters into the nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
This explains the six phrases of the sūtra beginning with "eternally free from desire.
Furthermore, regarding the statement, "All sensations (*vedanā*) are like the shadow of the tree of consciousness," etc.:
Because consciousness exists, sensation exists.
Sensation is described as a reflection;
why, then, is it referred to specifically as "sensation"?
Because craving is the root from which arises craving for sense objects and so forth,
and because the remaining bases are eternally extinguished, it is called "purified.
This refers to the purification of that consciousness when one attains *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*).
Because after entering parinirvāṇa, it cannot be said that there is purity;
furthermore, it is called "purity" because there is no consciousness, not because it exists as something named "purity.
Below, it explains that consciousness does not abide in consciousness.
According to the Abhidharma,
there is not even a single consciousness-nature within a single moment that can abide or be abided in;
yet this present commentary states:

Regarding the statement that "the intrinsic nature of the various consciousnesses is not defiled because the Blessed One taught that the nature of all minds is fundamentally pure," the intent is to clarify that the substance of consciousness is not of the nature of afflictions and is thus said to be non-defiled; that is, because the nature of mind is not an affliction, it is termed "fundamentally pure."
Because its nature is pure, the power of craving does not draw consciousness to abide therein.
The subsequent explanation—"Why is this so? ... down to 'all afflictions'"—means that afflictions such as greed are ultimately impure.
Because it is not an affliction (*kleśa*), one cannot say that it is ultimately impure.
This refers to the process within the continuity of the stream where one abandons contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) and attains uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).
Since it is likewise not an affliction, it does not exclusively serve as a causal condition for afflictions, just like form (*rūpa*) or sensation (*vedanā*).
This addresses an external objection.
The objection states:
"Just as the natures of form, sensation, and so forth are not themselves afflictions, yet they give rise to greed and the like, causing consciousness to dwell with pleasure."
Since consciousness itself is not an affliction, why does it not give rise to craving and so forth to cause consciousness to dwell in pleasure?
To resolve this objection,
it is said that each of the four aggregates, such as form and the rest, arises individually.
Because the afflictions are powerful, they are established as the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Consciousness, however, cannot by itself serve as the causal condition for afflictions in the same way that form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth do. Why is this?
Because there is certainly no instance where one gives rise to defiled attachment toward the nature of consciousness alone as one does toward form and so forth;
the nature of consciousness is subtle and cannot be seen,
and thus consciousness itself cannot produce defiled attachment.

The substance of the aggregate of form is coarse, and because the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations are coarse in their activity and engagement, they give rise to defiled craving through conditions.
Even if one were to experience defiled feeling toward consciousness, it must depend on form and the other aggregates before becoming defiled toward consciousness.
These four stations of consciousness are mostly explained in terms of consciousness itself;
their bases of stationing are the three aggregates associated with the six consciousnesses, as well as form.
Regardless of whether the manas takes the ālayavijñāna as an object of attachment or as an obstacle,
[the following] question is raised within the section on "Diverse Characteristics": Question:
Explanation. Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*),
there are five within the explanation.
First, the ten pairs of minds, such as those with greed and those without greed;
second, the twelve minds;
third, the twenty minds.
The fourth [section] clarifies the sixteen moments of mind;
the fifth provides a fivefold analysis of the first ten pairs of minds.
As for the statement, "the mind with greed and the mind free from greed, the mind with hatred and the mind free from hatred," and so forth:
Grasping and freedom from grasping; delusion and freedom from delusion;
distraction and non-distraction;
lethargy and freedom from lethargy.
Agitation and non-agitation;
tranquility and non-tranquility;
a concentrated mind and an unconcentrated mind.
"The mind that is cultivated and the mind that is not cultivated," as explained at length in the sūtra up to "the mind that is not liberated and the mind that is utterly liberated"—
this is the tenth pair.
This clarifies the distinctions among the ten remedial minds.
Regarding the four minds of the desire realm, the *Ki* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) states:
Within those five consciousnesses, there are only three types of mind;
there is no obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mind,
because such a characteristic cannot be apprehended.
If one is in the higher realms,
this neutral [state] exists within the five consciousnesses;
this obscured-neutral [state], however, exists only in the mental ground (manobhūmi).
The path of seeing is exclusively unwholesome.
Regarding the path of cultivation, if it gives rise to misconduct, it is unwholesome;
if it moistens rebirth or pertains to other such matters, it is neutral.
The remainder may be understood.
Regarding the twenty moments of mind,
Jing says:
Among these, the transformation-mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the desire realm is exclusively obtained through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*).
It can transform by means of minds of all three moral natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*),
unlike the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā) position which holds that there is a mind resulting from cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala-citta*) in the desire realm.
Furthermore, it says:
"The formless realm is also like this," which follows from the preceding [argument] by analogy that there is no *śailpasthānika-citta* (artistic or technical mind) there.
One should know that in the formless realm, there are likewise no minds of deportment or transformation.
Regarding the statement that "wholesome minds are the same whether inferior or superior," this refers generally to both types of wholesome minds:
those produced through application (*prāyogika*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).
Master Ji said:
"As in other places where the unobscured [neutral] has five types,
why is the neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*) not discussed here?"
The commentary states:
Its intrinsic nature is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), consisting of the material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) such as those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*) or those that are outflows (*naiṣyandika*).
Herein, it clarifies why the mind does not arise therein.
If that is so, under which category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) are such mental states as the grasping at phenomena subsumed?
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, they belong to the class of those produced by maturation (vipākaja).
It is subsumed under the neutral state of maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*).
The [neutral states] such as those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) are to be understood accordingly.
Although the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) exists in the desire realm, [it is not included here].
However, it is not a supernormal fruit (abhijñā-phala),
because there is no preparatory application (prayoga);
for a mind that is a supernormal fruit necessarily arises from preparatory application.
Because at the time of entering meditative absorption it is not a preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the desire realm,
the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) is not bound to the desire realm;
it consists solely of emanations such as those of devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.
It is exclusively acquired at birth;
that is to say, it can transform into various types of emanations such as human forms and so forth,
and it is not born of karmic maturation (vipāka).
If that is so, when the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth of the four levels transform things in the desire realm— such as manifesting various forms like humans—
what realm does this transformed matter (*rūpa*) belong to?
The commentary says:
The mind that follows the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) is bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta). If that is so, [then...]
How can the coarse eyes of a lower stage see the subtle forms of a higher stage?
The meaning is this:
the forms of the higher stages serve as the basis.
Above, it transforms separately into a type of matter belonging to the desire realm so that the eyes of those in the desire realm below can see it.
This transformed matter, which belongs to the desire realm, remains bound to the form realm because it was produced by the vision of one in the form realm.
Or rather, they are subtle phenomena (*sūkṣmadharma*).
How can they be made to be seen?
It is by way of their being of a coarse category (*audārikajātīya*).
This is why they are made visible.
In the formless realm, there is neither body nor deportment.
The treatise says:
Just as in the form realm there are no arts and crafts, and one does not speak of deportment or transformations,
these are omitted here for brevity.
As for those that are likewise absent in the higher realms:
Regarding this, the *Treatise* states,
as in the eighteenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
"In the formless realm, [these] are excluded, except for transformations and deportment."
Thus, one should know this briefly.
Some say that by this it is proven that the formless realm possesses transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and deportment-minds (*airyāpathika-citta*),
just like the meditative minds of the formless realm.
He attains great mastery over all forms and possesses the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*). There are bodhisattvas who,
relying on that meditative concentration, give rise to and abide in its practice.
Just as with Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above, what prevents them from also possessing a mind of deportment?
These are all wholesome and untainted (anāsrava). If that is so—
That is to say, it is comprised within the mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*) and so forth;
because it is a mind that produces similar transformations,
it is called a "mind of transformation" (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
Just as there is no neutral state for the mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) when it produces neutral states of maturation (*vipāka*) or deportment (*airyāpathika*),
so too it does not exist in that stage;
this refers to the discourse concerning ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the three vehicles.
It is not restricted to the inconceivable;
therefore, it is said that "it is also thus. Cè says:
Because the transformations of majestic deportment (īryāpatha) penetrate the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they are termed "twenty minds.
This is because the treatise does not make such a distinction.
In the detailed analysis of the ten pairs,
it is said that there are three categories:
first, the category of those who have not yet set out toward meditative concentration.
This refers to those in the desire realm who have not yet sought meditative concentration;
and second, those who, although they have already set out [on the path], have not yet attained the category of concentration—
that is, those who are currently seeking concentration.
Third, those who have already attained meditative concentration (samādhi).
These are further divided into two types:
first, those who are not yet pure.
This means that by subduing the afflictions, one attains the *anāgamya* concentration;
second, extreme purity,
which refers to attaining the fundamental dhyānas.
In the first chapter,
at times the three pairs of defiled minds— greed, hatred, and delusion— arise together;
at other times, wholesome or neutral minds arise.
Because one is distanced from the fetters of greed and so forth,
the mere non-occurrence of greed and so forth is itself termed non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
The *anāgamya-samādhi* (preparatory concentration) is necessarily a wholesome state of mind;
it may also be neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the second category, it is said that at times, when the mind is not properly settled upon its object, it becomes agitated (*uddhata*) and so forth.
Master Ji said:
"According to the eight entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), there is also *kaukṛtya* (remorse/worry).
When practicing tranquility (*śamatha*), torpor (*styāna*) and sleep (*middha*) act as obstacles; the same applies when practicing insight (*vipaśyanā*)."
In this context, non-quiescence is omitted for brevity.
If it were simply equated with the two factors of dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), what would be the point?
Because they obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*), that which is quiescent is equanimity itself.
Otherwise, envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) would have to be taken as its essential nature,
because it is stated as such among the *paryavasthānas* and *nīvaraṇas*.
This is the sequence of the fourth aggregate (*skandha*).
In the middle [section], first the sequence is distinguished according to five meanings;
subsequently, it is distinguished based on two matters.
Regarding the preceding section:
as there are many sequential arrangements in the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*,
I shall not cite them all here for fear of being overly tedious.
Although there are five meanings within this context,
such that form comes first and consciousness last, the reason for their sequence is as follows:
among the five types of sequential order of arising and function, the aggregate of form is explained first and the aggregate of consciousness second.
The eye and visible forms as conditions constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
That which gives rise to visual consciousness constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Based upon these forms and consciousness, mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) arise.
Based on this sequence, form, consciousness, feeling, perception, and mental formations are explained in this very order.
Within the second sequence of antidotes,
the third [antidote] is for the inversion regarding the self.
Jingyun: This differs from the Lesser Treatise’s reckoning of the mind as permanent;
here it is stated that non-Buddhists reckon the mind as the self.
Therefore, consciousness is the third [link].
As for those who conceive the impermanent as permanent:
Taking the aggregates of perception and formations together as permanent,
perception constitutes the fourth and formations the fifth.
Jizang says:
"This [statement] is based on the fact that the mind is regarded as a self through the conceptualization of the majority of discriminative thought; therefore, it is a distortion regarding the mind.
In other passages, it is based on the fact that all innate [thoughts] regard things as a self; therefore, it is a distortion regarding phenomena."
Both of these are obtained.
Within the third [section], the sequence of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*),
the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is the first.
Feeling is the second;
perception is the third.
Perception grasps the images, characteristics, names, and colors of objects.
The fourth [member] is action.
The first is that which is fulfilled;
this is consciousness, the fifth.
Within the systematic arrangement,
the former is explained in detail and the latter is summarized concisely.
That which is established as what is cognized is form (*rūpa*).
That which possesses suffering and pleasure is feeling (*vedanā*).
That which arises following verbal expression is perception (*saṃjñā*).
"Both the foolish and the wise engage in this practice.
The term "and so forth" (etc. includes consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The following section establishes the sequence based on two matters.
The first four aggregates are established based on the objects that serve as the equipment for the self;
the final aggregate of consciousness is established based on the entity of the self itself.
That is to say, it is the self that relies upon the body.
That which is form is the object;
that which experiences pleasure and pain within those various objects is sensation.
That which arises as verbal expression regarding oneself or others is perception (*saṃjñā*).
These two types [of perception] can only be accumulated based upon what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
These two, sensation and perception, are able to accumulate only by depending upon the factors that are either dharma or non-dharma within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Fifth, the explanation of inclusion (*saṃgraha*) follows.
Among these:
First, the six types of inclusion are explained;
next, the ten types of inclusion are explained;
finally, the demarcation of the methods for excluding and including is explained.
To begin with:
regarding the statement that the form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) comprises a portion of six of the members of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga*),
this refers to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Name-and-form,
the six sense bases,
birth, aging, and death, and the principles of possibility and impossibility (sthānāsthāna) apply to all phenomena.
Now, taking only form (*rūpa*) is also called "a partial portion.
As for the seven faculties taken in their entirety,
these refer to the five material faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*).
As well as the male and female faculties.

birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Regarding "those who do not restrain their faculties," Ji says:
they are not considered faculties because they are obscured by wisdom.

For instance, when one recollects a past event, it is said that wisdom (prajñā) recollects; because this occurs through the process of subsequent conceptualization (paryavasthāna), it is not a faculty (indriya).

as for the partial inclusion of five of the branches of existence,
these refer to volitional formations, name-and-form, birth, and old age and death.

the three faculties in part refer to [the remaining faculties].
The three untainted [factors].

it refers to the constituent of consciousness (vijñānāṅga).
A portion of the four members of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), namely:
name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
These are not called "existence" (*bhava*).
Because of the existence of karma,
one faculty is complete;
namely, the mental faculty (*manas*).
A small portion of the three faculties—

Next, the ten types of inclusion will be explained.
Regarding "included within the realms":
this refers to the inclusion of the effect by means of its cause.

Regarding "inclusion by category" (*jāti-saṃgraha*), this refers to things being subsumed under their own respective categories, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
