likewise, past and future forms, though not themselves resistant, are called "form" because they belong to the category of the resistant.
Even the consciousness-bodies of the past and future are called "consciousness" because they belong to the category of discernment (*vijñapti*).

As for those included by way of state (*avasthā*), it is like when a pleasant feeling arises: the preceding and succeeding aggregates that accord with that pleasant feeling are collectively termed the "aggregate of pleasure," and so forth.
Regarding the inclusion by way of non-separation (*avinirbhāga-saṃgraha*),
the Tripiṭaka Master says:
"It refers to the fact that within a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-puñja*), there are as many included elements (*dhātu*) and so forth as exist in a state of non-separation."
Master Ji said:
"According to the Abhidharma,
all phenomena that possess form are likewise inseparable from the mind."
Therefore, all are matter.
Mental factors are also called "mind and so forth.
Regarding their inclusion by time:
The past includes the past, up to and including a single moment;
this is what is meant by "included within the intermediate.
Alternatively, it refers to that which arises based upon this [moment].
This refers to "consciousness arises dependent on form," and so forth.
Regarding the complete inclusion [of the aggregates] therein, Master Ji said:

Regarding the statement that the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), are "phenomena that encompass meaning" (*saṃgrāhaka-dharma*), the answer is that they fully encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Jñānaprasthāna-bhāṣya states:
"These include all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aggregates, as well as the aggregates of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*)," and so forth.
All are subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Regarding those subsumed by way of a partial inclusion,
Jing says:
As it is said: "All forms (rūpa) comprise a portion of the aggregates (skandha), and so on, up to all consciousnesses (vijñāna) comprising a portion of the aggregates.
Furthermore, within the aggregate of form, there are eleven types.
Taking only one type is called "inclusion by a small portion.
As for inclusion by the ultimate meaning:
Subsuming phenomena through principle,
all dharmas are exhausted;
there is not a single dharma that exists outside of suchness.
Next is the section on the gate of exclusion.
Jing says: "As it is said, 'excluding the aggregate of form' (rūpaskandha)."
Are the remaining aggregates included within the aggregates, elements, and bases?
Answer:
They include the four aggregates in their entirety.
The seven elements in their entirety,
a portion of the dharma-element,
and the mind-base in its entirety.
A portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Excluding the sphere of phenomena,
all remaining spheres subsume the spheres of faculties, bases, and aggregates.
The commentary states:
It subsumes seventeen elements (dhātus) and eleven bases (āyatanas) in their entirety.
The entirety of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) and a portion of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha),
excluding the sense-base of mind (mano-āyatana).
How many bases, aggregates, and elements are subsumed within the remaining bases?
Answer:
The ten bases in their entirety.
The four aggregates in their entirety and the ten elements in their entirety;
at this time, from among the three categories of phenomena, one takes a single phenomenon from each to encompass all phenomena exhaustively.
This means that by taking up the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), one fully includes the ten elements (*dhātu*) and ten bases (*āyatana*) of form,
as well as a portion of one [element and base]. By taking up the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),

one fully includes the element of phenomena, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and the entirety of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, and saṃskāraskandha*).
Furthermore, it comprises a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
namely the five kinds of form within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*),
because they are included within the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).
This includes the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the element of mind (*cittadhātu*).
If one takes up the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
it includes eleven kinds of form.
If one takes the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu),
it subsumes eighty-seven dharmas;
that is to say, fifty-three mental factors (caitta).
Matter is of two kinds:
matter of restraint and non-restraint, as well as matter that is the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
There are twenty-four kinds of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
There are eight unconditioned phenomena.
If one takes the sense-base of mind (manāyatana),
it subsumes the seven mental elements (cittadhātu) and the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
Regarding the sixth section,
"Clarifying the Bases," concerning the transformation of the aggregate of form within the six sense bases among the bases:
Jing says:
First, the construction of houses and the like;
second, walls, enclosures, clothing, and the like;
third, requisites such as beds, stools, food, drink, and other articles.
The fourth consists of the five sense faculties;
the fifth consists of the objective fields that support those faculties;
and the sixth consists of the matter of the determined sphere.
Basibandhu says:
"One" refers to the earth, the golden wheel, and so forth;
"three and two" refer to houses, walls, and so forth.
The third refers to clothing, beds, and so forth;
the fourth refers to the sense faculties; the fifth refers to the supports for the sense faculties.
The sixth refers to the abode of the meditative concentrations of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
It does not mention the matter of non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) and so forth, nor the matter produced by mastery over concentration (*vaśitā-samādhi*),
because these are not fully subsumed under the distinct categories of afflictions.
Regarding the phrase "turning based on the seven bases and four aggregates," Ji says:
What is the difference between desire (*chanda*) and aspiration (*āśā*)?
First, regarding objects already attained;
second, regarding objects not yet attained—
that is, taking as objects future or past births as appropriate.
"Object-sphere" refers to the object-spheres that function spontaneously in the present.
"Investigation and analysis" refers to...
Although the aforementioned sūtras also contain vitarka and vicāra, their functions are distinct.
Vitarka and vicāra arise only with respect to objects that have been thought about, whether already attained or not yet attained; they do not arise otherwise.
Furthermore, regarding those who desire harmony and so forth:
because they long for harmony,
these renunciants of the desire realm [act as follows].
This is subsumed within the investigation and analysis of this sphere.
Those who enjoy sensual desires rely upon four bases;
those who abide in restraint rely upon clear comprehension.
One who has already attained the preparatory concentration (sāmantaka-samādhi) relies upon the pure means of practice;
one who abides in the fundamental concentration (maula-samādhi) [relies upon the same].
Relying on purity.
Above, within the expertise regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*), the analysis of the aggregates according to six meanings has been completed.
From here below, secondly, the expertise regarding the aggregates is clarified by means of the two meanings of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Among these, that which is about to be analyzed first permits the explanation of form,
and only thereafter is it explained.
Regarding the analysis of form (*rūpa*),
first the question is posed and then it is explained.
Within the explanation, a single verse is first cited to enumerate its ten categories.
The sequential explanation consists of ten points:

first, the single entity; second, the subtle; third, the arising; fourth, the establishment; fifth, the flow; sixth, the activity; seventh, the momentary; eighth, the solitary; ninth, the sphere of activity; and tenth, the intermingling.
The analysis of entities according to seven gates begins with clarifying the quantity of things occupying the same location.
Regarding the question, "How many entities are comprised within the eye of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)? [the following is explained].
"Things" refers to the substance; "matters" refers to the meaning of the question.
For instance, within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), by how many elements is the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) subsumed?
Answer: If,
according to inclusion by characteristic (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*), there is only a single entity and so forth,
then if it is clarified by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it includes only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
This means that the basis of visual consciousness is cited as the result to indicate its cause.
As for the statement that there are seven substances according to the inclusion of those that are inseparable,
this refers to their being inseparable by virtue of occupying the same location.
The Supplementer says:
Generally, there are three ways in which things are explained as being inseparable:
first, inseparability by virtue of occupying the same location.
This refers to the eye-faculty being produced as a result of prior karma.
At the moment of birth, as the eye-faculty is about to arise,
the earth element first arises and occupies its location.
Subsequently, when reaching the stage of the "limb of the locus of loss," the eye-faculty first arises;
at that same time and in the same location,
there subsequently arise the body-faculty, the earth-element, and the four objects that support the faculties.
In this way, these seven substances combine to form a single entity that is universally interpenetrating.
It is like lighting many lamps within a single room; their forms are universally interpenetrating in a manner that cannot be described as being "here" or "there."
It is also like peach and other fruits: when they grow, regardless of their size, their substance is a single unity and cannot be said to be an accumulation of many atoms.
This is called "being in the same location without separation."
Regarding the principle that these seven substances can exist in the same location without being separated from one another, they must be of the same nature;
that is to say, those of the nature of maturation (vipāka) are of the same maturation,
and those of the nature of growth (aupacayika) are of the same growth.
If the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) are viewed as being of different natures,
they are subsumed under the categories of "intermingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) and "not separated" (*avinirbhāga*),
such as in a heap of rice or barley.
This is called the "conjunction and non-separation" inclusion.
Regarding the first question:
it is like the retributive eye, the nurtured eye-faculty, and the two kinds of objects and great elements.
Since they occupy the same location within a single body and are not distinct, it cannot be said that one is "here" and the other "there.
While the retribution [of the fruit] resides internally, the nourishment [of the cause] dwells externally;
yet, if these internal and external aspects were mutually pervasive, there would be no distinction between their locations.
What is meant by "not being in different locations yet not being separated"?
The explanation says:
retributive matter (*vipākaja-rūpa*) is coarse.
The intermediate space accommodates and nurtures the sense faculties and the great elements;
just as water and sand differ in nature and category despite occupying the same location,
they cannot be said to be "co-spatial and inseparable."
This is because the two faculties of the matured [retribution], the two great elements, and the four kinds of objects obstruct one another and do not interpenetrate;
whereas the matured great elements and the matured faculties and objects are mutually pervasive in their own essence and occupy the same location.
When the nourishing earth element and the nourishing sense faculties and objects mutually pervade one another's own characteristics,
this is called "being in the same location without separation.
This is because it is the natural law of these two great elements that they are mutually obstructive.
The two types of matter and the two types of fragrance, and so forth, likewise obstruct one another.
Therefore, the retribution-born and the nurtured cannot be separated from each other; this is why they are said to be "coexistent and inseparable.
This is the second question.
Just as the gods of the Heaven of Equal Mind possess immense bodies,
they came to where the Buddha was, each occupying a space the size of a single hair-tip.
Since their substance is pervasive, they enter one another, and their locations are not distinct;
furthermore, as they are equally retributive fruits,
why are they not termed "mutually non-separable by virtue of being in the same location"?
The commentary states:
The retributive form of those devas is pure like the light of a lamp, such that they do not obstruct or hinder one another;
nevertheless, each perceives it according to their own karma.
Since their respective boundaries are different,
they cannot be said to be "in the same location and inseparable," nor can it be said that they have been in one and the same place from beginning to end.
Those devas are not like this;
their gathering and dispersing are not constant,
and therefore they do not occupy the same location.
The third question:
It is already known that being inseparable from the same location must be their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
however, regarding retribution (*vipāka*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), they are merely mixed in terms of designation (*nāma*).
It is not yet known whether these combined characteristics aggregate to form a coarse entity,
or whether each object arises individually according to its size rather than being formed by aggregation.
The explanation states:
Now, the Mahāyāna teaches that all internal and external forms arise according to prior karma;
regardless of their size, each is a single entity and not a composite of many parts.
This is the fourth question.

The manifested body—consisting of hair, fur, nails, teeth, and so forth from head to foot—is composed of the four elements (mahābhūta) as results of maturation (vipākaja) and nourishment (aupacayika), and is a provisional composite of many parts.
How can it be said that this arises as a single entity rather than being a collection?
The commentary states:
Although these various colors differ in their intrinsic natures,
through the power of causes and conditions, they arise simultaneously in a single location as a single entity.
It is not like soil, which first separates when not yet mixed with water and later combines its fine particles to form a coarse mass;
therefore, it is said that a single entity arises according to its size.
This was the fifth question.
If the integrated whole were not a single entity,
how could it later be cut and divided into many parts by knives and axes?
The explanation says:
Later, when encountering the conditions for destruction by knives and axes,
the fundamental whole perishes as a single entity,
while numerous subtle parts arise through the conditions of the knives and axes.
It does not mean that a single entity from a previous time is entirely broken and cut into many;
for this reason, the most subtle form of matter, the *paramāṇu*, is not established within the Mahāyāna.
The sixth question asks again:
For what reason does the Mahāyāna not admit that the most subtle atoms (paramāṇu) aggregate to form sense faculties and objects?
Even if one were to admit such aggregation, what fault would there be?
The commentary states:
All sentient beings produce eyes from karma, intended for the function of seeing.
The ear arises from karma with the capacity for hearing;
the same applies to the other faculties.
Thus, those eyes and so forth arise from karma as complete entities, producing the functional capacity of their respective sense organs.
The five sense objects are likewise; they must arise as complete entities from prior karma to function as objective spheres.
You yourself also agree that the most subtle atoms do not constitute sense organs or objects.
How can those useless atoms arise from karma,
only to later require accumulation before they can constitute sense organs and objects?
Therefore, does the Hīnayāna school not labor in vain by establishing subtle atoms, expending effort on a pursuit that yields no practical utility?

Furthermore, this teaching accords with the Vaiśeṣika position that permanent atoms are not destroyed at the end of a kalpa, but subsequently assemble from subtle to coarse during the kalpa of formation.

The subsequent passage states that when a mass of form first arises, it arises as a whole; when it finally perishes, it does not reach the state of atoms. Thus, its intermediate destruction is established as being like that of a drop of water.
It further states:
"Furthermore, when various aggregates of matter arise, they are like various substances ground into powder and formed into a mass by mixing with water;
they do not arise as a mere collection like mustard seeds, wheat, or beans."
Why is this? Because it arises through the predominant power of its respective cause of birth,
and thus it arises so as to be functional.
Seventh: If there are no real atoms within the Mahāyāna, for what reason does it further teach the contemplation of subtle atoms?
Answer:
In order to destroy sentient beings' attachment to the mind as being substantially real,
he taught the analytical deconstruction [of the body] from head to foot as a collection of various subtle particles.
By performing this contemplation, one gives rise to the mental image of space regarding internal and external forms, thereby conforming to the three gates of liberation.
Sthiramati says:
Just as the seven atoms belonging to a single visual faculty occupy the same location at the same time without obstructing one another,
a single atom of the visual faculty is as large as a grape.
Within this, each subtle particle can accommodate other ultimate particles;
thus, proceeding in this manner, it is extensively explained that within a single aggregate there exist those seven substances.
If one speaks according to the actual reality,
since there is no separate substance for the atom, how can there be seven objects?
The explanation says:
Just as the color of a grape is a pure color,
that which serves as the function of seeing is called the eye; likewise,
up to that which serves as the function of touching is called touch.
All [aggregates] can be reduced to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Therefore, it is said that there are seven ultimate atoms within a single cluster;
it is not that there are seven actual entities within a real ultimate atom.
This refers to their being inseparable while occupying the same location.
Now, as for these three types of inseparability, are they taught according to the Hīnayāna or do they represent the meaning of the Mahāyāna?
Regarding this, there are two interpretations.
Master Bei’s intention lies in the Mahāyāna, and he likewise holds this view:
if all were categorized according to their realms (*dhātu*), there would be seven entities and so forth;
for the realm is the seed.
Although the elements of water, fire, and wind do not exist within the locus of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), their seeds reside within the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

This is based on the period prior to the establishment of the teaching of the *ālayavijñāna*, wherein the seeds of the three great elements were held to reside within the five faculties, the six consciousnesses, and the mental factors (*caitta*) of the earth and fire bases.
Second, it is explained that derived tangible objects are conventional (prajñapti).
Within this, first,
the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent topic is introduced.
The second explanation states:
Jing says that all twenty kinds of tangibles are conventionally established based on the various states of the four great elements.
Baso says:
"In this context, there are nineteen types of contact explained;
they are like the twenty-two types found in the Abhidharma."
There are no three [qualities] of haste, slowness, or inferiority.
Why are they absent?
Because they are abbreviated.
Birth is not established as the cause of contact.
For example, among the four characteristics, sickness and old age are one;
why then are these two divided here?
Now, this is not one of the four characteristics;
it is not analogous.
As for that which is touched by death:
Named according to their effects:
when these vital points (*marmans*) on the body are struck,
they cause death immediately.
This contact is named after its fruit;
the same applies to the contact of aging.
This contact is capable of producing aging and so forth.
This is called "contact with the aged.
As for the statement that the six stages are further divided into eight and so forth,
it means that the first two— purity and impurity— are counted as two.
The firm and the non-firm constitute a duality;
thus there are eight.
Third, this clarifies how the various consciousnesses apprehend objects, both collectively and individually.
Regarding the statement "either gradual or sudden," Ji says:
this means that when any one of the five consciousnesses arises together with the mental consciousness (manas) to take an object, it is called "gradual."
If the five consciousnesses arise simultaneously and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) likewise takes the same object, this is called "simultaneous" (*tun*).
Fourth, it clarifies that in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are no two objects nor two consciousnesses.
Master Ji says:
What is the purpose of these faculties?
The meaning is that,
according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, they serve to adorn the body.
The commentary says:
If one adorns the body so as to sufficiently support the sense organs and their objects, [it is permissible].
What is the function of the sense organs?
The explanation says:
To produce vocal sounds, one must rely on the support of the sense organs and their objects.
If there is that which can rely upon the eye faculty,
and the object upon which it relies is present, only then will speech be produced based on it;
otherwise, it cannot be obtained.
Therefore, the sense-faculties are necessary;
even up to the case of the faculties of the formless realm,
they likewise have no physical basis.
Regarding the second point, the refutation that if the two faculties do not exist, their locus also does not exist,
and so forth— this should be understood by reversing the sequence of the enumeration.
The fifth section clarifies the meaning of the twelve kinds of conventional designations for form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the statement, "Among all such forms, nine are substantially existent," Ki states:
"In the subsequent text..."
Just as within the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), dimensions such as length and so forth are conventional (*prajñapti*), while blue and yellow are substantial (*dravya*);

likewise, among sounds, those caused by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and those not caused by the primary elements are substantial, while others, such as pleasant sounds and so forth, are conventional.
Among fragrances, those that are agreeable to the mind are conventional (prajñapti), while the arising of the combination of various factors through other conditions is real (dravya).
Among tastes, the six such as bitter and sour are real, whereas other agreeable tastes and so forth are conventional.
Within each and every atom, there are both the provisional and the real.
Why is it that here, even up to the ninth [category], it is said that all possess the "tangible portion" (*spraṣṭavya-aṃśa*) in two ways?
The meaning is as follows:
Because within the sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), there is a distinction between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
and because all derived matter is merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*),
it is explained in detail for these reasons, as it is also manifold.
Among the remaining nine [bases], there is no derived matter that acts as a creator;
furthermore, they are all derived matter.
Although among derived matter there are those that are nominal (prajñapti), [they are still derived].
However, they are minor and not numerous;
therefore, they are not discussed. Cè says:
The various tangibles, such as smoothness and so forth, have no distinct derived matter apart from the primary elements that constitute them;
because they are designated as "derived" based on those very primary elements, they are called "provisional.
Although dimensions such as long and short are also provisionally existent, they are established by depending upon the derived matter that is itself provisionally constructed.
That which depends upon its basis is not called "provisionally existent.

Regarding the two types of matter included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-rūpa): if it possesses majestic power and is an object of meditative concentration, such as a transformation (nirmāṇa) and so forth; [it is the first type].
Bei Jing also states:
"The meditative state of mind of the sages of the Three Vehicles refers to the manifestation within the heart when one practices the eight *kṛtsnāyatana* (all-pervading) contemplations."
This is substantially existent.
It serves as a condition for others by causing them to perceive the eightfold aspects of their own mind's transformations.
Just as a transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) gives rise to transformative matter (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*) which serves as a condition for others and causes them to see the matter transformed by oneself.
The manifest form is the fruit of the concentrated mind;
the subsequent [form] is the object of that concentration and is thus called the objective sphere (*ālambana*).
Therefore, it is asked: "Is it the fruit of that, and is it the object of that?"
Since the object traversed by meditative concentration is already the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
how can it be seen by the eyes of others?
Answer:
It is because it acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to cause others to transform themselves that visual consciousness sees;
it does not mean that it causes others to see the forms within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
Thus says Tái.
Regarding mastery over meditative concentration, it is said to possess "majestic power" (mahānubhāva), just as the five supernormal powers (abhijñā) are so named.
Because the objects traversed by concentration serve as conditions for others to perceive, hear, and so forth,
it is illustrated by the example of "magical transformation" (nirmāṇa).
It is called "the fruit" because the meditative state of mastery manifests due to long-term cultivation of concentration;
it is called "the object" because the sphere of the meditative frequency manifests through mental attention (*manasikāra*);
and it is called "and consciousness, etc. because it includes the matter associated with the remaining kings of the frequency.
Since each of the kings individually manifests within their own respective realms, they must be mentioned separately.
Ji says: "Among the forms of the dharma-base (dharmāyatana-rūpa)..."

As stated in the Abhidharma, there are two kinds of matter produced by mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*): that which arises from concentration possessing majestic power (*prabhāva*) and that which arises from concentration of mental construction (*parikalpa*) lacking such power.
Here, only concentration possessing majestic power is intended.
Regarding the five types of form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), four are entirely conventional and one part is real.
What is meant by "majestic power" (*vaibhutvika*) such that it is called real?
As stated in the following passage, because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is termed majestic power.
Because it is the dharma of the noble ones, it is called "majestic power" (tejas).
This meditative matter (dhyāna-rūpa) is capable of performing real functions,
just like transformed matter (nirmāṇa-rūpa).
That which is not the color produced by majestic power or meditative concentration merely causes others to see it; it does not actually perform a function,
unlike a transformation-body (*nirmāṇa*).
Question:
It is taught that untainted (anāsrava) form is attained only upon the realization of the truths (satyadarśana).
Since this [attainment] involves a slight degree of tainted (sāsrava) concentration, for what reason can such a substantial entity exist?
The Noble Ones obtain it because they belong to the lineage of those free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
As stated in the subsequent text, they obtain it through the dominant power (*adhipati-bala*).

Furthermore, according to the following passage, since subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises through the dominant power of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), this form cannot be obtained through contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*).
In this context, because the substance is actually untainted (*anāsrava*) while appearing similar to what is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is said to be the cause of both the untainted and the tainted.
Furthermore, the *Da yi* states:
"This applies to both the tainted and the untainted; however, that which is tainted is not real, as it is unfit for actual enjoyment."
If that which is not a conceptual construction were not functional, it would also be substantially existent.
Regarding the statement here, "that fruit and that object," the *Mahārtha* says:
As for the result, it is that which causes the fundamental consciousness to transform and manifest as objective objects through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is just as, after entering a Pure Land, the power of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) causes the fundamental consciousness to transform and manifest as objects.
This is precisely the actual existence of the fruit of meditative concentration.
It is because it is said to be the fruit of the mind,
and because it is the object of focus for that concentration.
Therefore, this concentrated form (samāhita-rūpa), when compared to concentration itself, is both its fruit and its object, yet it is a single entity.
Question:
Is it only the form that is the object of a single number within concentration that exists as a substantial reality?
At the same time, that which is transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) also exists as a real entity.
Therefore, it says, "and those associated with it," etc.,
which serves to resolve doubts and difficulties.
Among these, only three types are established within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Therefore, both the matter of restraint and non-restraint are merely conventional designations,
as they are established based upon volition and other such factors.

Furthermore, regarding the matter of whether the forms traversed in meditative concentration (samādhi) are produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to the same realm as the concentration upon which they depend:

Jing says, "This passage is based on the fact that when one gives rise to [forms] induced from the form realm (rūpadhātu), they are produced by the primary elements of the form realm; thus it states that they are freely produced by those elements."

Because the formless realm lacks the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), one cannot say that the matter manifested by the concentration bound to the formless realm depends upon the great elements bound to the formless realm.

Therefore, the subsequent passage explains that the matter which is the fruit of superior concentration, subsumed under the "place of dharma," depends solely upon superior concentration and not upon the great elements.

Nevertheless, because it arises from a samādhi that has as its object an image of that same kind, it is also said to be derived from those primary elements (*mahābhūta*) but not produced based upon them.

This is like when one sees a blue mat outside of meditative concentration and subsequently enters concentration, wherein one contemplates the blue seen previously as an image of blue appearing within the concentrated mind.

Furthermore, that which arises as such, produced through the predominant influence of karma of this particular kind—
This is due to karma that there are many atoms within the space of a single particle.
How is it known that there are many?
Because all aggregates of matter and all material sense-faculties are collectively experienced [by them].
Within any aggregate of matter,
if one were to select the most minute and subtle object, it would still possess all [eight] atoms;
when the eye sees this form, [it perceives it as such].
This is because the nose perceives fragrance,
the tongue tastes flavor,
and the body experiences touch.
The counter-argument from below can be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover,
there are various forms" addresses the second objection regarding non-obstructiveness.
Alternatively, there may be mutual obstruction in this location;
for example, two atoms of earth, or two substances, two odors, or two tangibles of the same nature, necessarily do not interpenetrate one another.
Regarding "not mutually obstructing one another in this location":
it is like the earth and its four qualities, each being simply one and thus not obstructing one another.
As for those who possess form within,
it is like one possessing form within seeking a place of rebirth;
they pass straight through rocky mountains without obstruction.
If there is an obstacle to the intermediate state (antarābhava),
or if it cannot pass upon entering the mother’s womb,
this constitutes an obstruction.
Regarding the establishment of the absence of parts:
as stated in the third fascicle of the *Maulī Bhūmi*,
"It is not the case that further subtle parts can be found within an atom," and so forth.
Third, it clarifies whether those five eyes perceive or do not perceive the five distinct types of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Jñānagarbha says:
"The two eyes—the flesh eye and the divine eye—arise in dependence upon light and darkness."
Therefore, the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) is not seen.
As for the essential nature of the three eyes— wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others—
the Tripiṭaka Master says:
The wisdom-eye takes emptiness as its object;
the dharma-eye takes existence as its object;
both are subsequently attained wisdoms.
The Buddha-eye must necessarily have a distinct essence;

Because it is only at the stage of the fruit that [the name] is applied.

how could it take atoms as its object?

it can also take atoms themselves as its object.

Thus says the Tripiṭaka Master.

Moreover, this interpretation is not correct.

while the dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) taking emptiness and existence as its object is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*),
the Buddha eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) subsumes these two preceding ones to constitute the Buddha eye.
How is this known?
As the Abhidharma states, suchness is exclusively the object of the noble eye of wisdom;
therefore, we know that the eye of wisdom takes suchness as its object.

Because it is said to be "pure," it takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its object.

The Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) is a synonym for this [wisdom], and because it takes wisdom as its essence, it is called the "Wisdom-eye" (*prajñācakṣus*).
This is not the Wisdom-eye among the five eyes;
while in the causal stage, it is termed the "Dharma-wisdom."
In terms of the fruit, they are collectively named "Buddha.

According to the words of the fiftieth [chapter],

There are three interpretations:
first, the aforementioned four eyes, upon attaining the ultimate perfection of a Buddha, are all termed the Buddha-eye.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
the three preceding sections constitute the completion of the first part: the exposition of the definitive meaning.
From this point downward, the errors are refuted.
First, there is a general question and answer;

Regarding the preceding point:
it is like a drop of water that does not reach the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Furthermore, as for the statement that the analogy of a drop of water reaching a minute form (*sūkṣmarūpa*) is not the case here—it is indeed so.
Regarding the five characteristics,
Tai states that the first three are the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda.
The fourth is the position held by the Sautrāntikas, the Sthaviras, and others:
that the derived aggregate of matter (upādāyarūpa) abides by accumulating within the infinitesimal particles (paramāṇu) of the four great elements (mahābhūta), with each interpenetrating the other.
Because it posits distinct atoms, it differs from the Mahāyāna;
because it allows for mutual interpenetration, it differs from the Sarvāstivāda;
and it is the calculation of the fifth heterodox school.
Sthiramati says:
"The first [position] refers to the Sarvāstivādins, who hold that although atoms do not exist in isolation,
their own nature exists within composite matter."
This correctly refutes the Sarvāstivādins and,
concurrently, refutes the Vaiśeṣikas;
the second [point] concerns arising and ceasing.
This refers precisely to the Sarvāstivādins,
who hold that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the parents of Vaiśeṣika are eternal while all else is impermanent;
now, this [view] is refuted as well.
The third is precisely the Vaiśeṣika school.
According to their tenet,
at the beginning of the kalpa, the parents and atoms were scattered and dwelling everywhere throughout the empty kalpa.
Later, during the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*), when a child is born from the union of parents, it is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) because of its subtle nature.
The fourth [school] is precisely the Sarvāstivāda,
because they maintain that the accumulation of matter is formed by the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Furthermore, it is said that this is the doctrine of the Saṃmitīya school,
because for them there are no atoms (paramāṇu), but rather only accumulated aggregates.
This is the fifth Vaiśeṣika [view].
Because the subtle elements of the parents harmoniously combine, they give rise to the various names of coarse aggregates of form;
since these subtle elements lack substantiality,
and because they lack substantiality, they are without arising or ceasing.
Because there is no arising or ceasing, there is neither conjunction nor dispersion.
One cannot say that aggregated matter arises from atoms and so forth.
By this principle, the five aforementioned views are all irrational.
Ce said: As stated in the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*,
when the Tathāgata had not yet attained the Way...
The master Andhaka, having studied the methods of calculation,
questioned his teacher, saying:
"How many atoms (*paramāṇu*) are there in Jambudvīpa?"
The Master of Verses replied:
"It cannot be expressed through calculation.
He asked:
Question: How many atoms (paramāṇu) constitute a kṣudraka?
Answer:
This, too, is not stated.
If it were thus,
there would be nothing further to learn.
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
Passing through worlds as numerous as motes of dust,
the *Acintya-sūtra* further states:
"All worlds enter into a single mote of dust."
Such is the holy teaching.
For what reason, then, is it said that there are no atoms (*paramāṇu*)?
The explanation is as follows:
The Sūtra speaks of their existence based on the atoms (*paramāṇu*) that constitute the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the mental consciousness;
the Śāstra states they do not exist with reference to the primary dharma itself.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
From here below, the third section clarifies that establishing the atom through provisional analysis yields five benefits.
Jì (基) states:
"The first is the benefit of attaining the destruction of the notion of permanence, thereby clarifying impermanence."
Second, because one knows impermanence,
one does not conceive of a self or what belongs to a self.
Third, since there is no self, [one does not conceive of what belongs to a self].
At that same time, the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) is also able to be severed and extinguished.
Having severed the view of a self and conceit in the fourth [dhyāna],
one does not give rise to various afflictions regarding those objects.
It causes [the afflictions] to remain suppressed and not manifest;
fifth, because it suppresses all delusions,
one does not grasp at signs within objects.
And one is able to eliminate the attachment to phenomena.
These five benefits are possessed by a distinct class of individuals;
they can be understood through reflection on their nature.
The Tripitaka Master says:
"The first is the gate of emptiness;
the middle three are the gate of wishlessness."
Next is the gate of signlessness.
Question:
For what reason is it that, after the second [gate] which refutes the self, one speaks of wishlessness?
Now, to further explain: the first two are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because they are subsumed under the practice of emptiness and the practice of selflessness (*anātman*).
The middle two are the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Jingyun: The first three are emptiness;
the next one is wishlessness.
The latter is the single gate of signlessness (*animitta*).
Within the ten gates, the third, the gate of origination (*utpatti*), has five parts.
First, the origination is distinguished by means of five meanings.
Second, it clarifies that [the primary elements] are intermingled yet inseparable;
third, it clarifies that although derived matter possesses its own seeds, it arises through the transformation of the primary elements;
fourth, it clarifies that the result undergoes transformation due to five conditions.
Fifth, the establishment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Among the first five meanings, it concerns the basis of arising;
that is to say, whatever other derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) exists within the location of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as its support.
At the time of initial birth,
the primary elements (mahābhūta) first occupy their respective locations;
other material forms arise dependent upon these primary elements.
"It is called 'arising based on a support' (āśraya-utpatti). 'That which, in the same location,
sustains that object' explains its meaning of 'construction' (nirmāṇa)."
Because the earth element sustains the matter that occupies the same location, it is called "formation" (*kṛta*).
Furthermore, if within this accumulation of matter there are characteristics ranging from existence to non-existence,
these are collectively distinguished as being or non-being.
That is to say, if within a collection of form there exists the earth element or any other primary element,
as well as derived matter, whether it be a sense faculty or an object,
then those phenomena are present.

If within a mass of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*) there were only one of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and no other three great elements, nor any derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), then that phenomenon would not exist.
As for what follows, if someone should say... [the text continues].
He cites their tenets to refute them.
The Sarvāstivādins and others say:
"All aggregates of matter must necessarily possess the four great elements."
Just as within a single stone, although the characteristics of the elements of fire, water, and wind cannot be perceived,
they must nonetheless exist in their ultimate atoms;
now, one should question them regarding this.
Regarding this earth element which is obtainable and the other three elements which are unobtainable:
are their natures equal or unequal?
If their essence were of a single kind,
it would be irrational for those three great elements to be unapprehendable. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
Within a single stone, the other elements— water, fire, and wind— should also be obtainable,
because their substance and so forth exist therein,
just as with the earth element.
If they are not equal, it is because they are unequal in terms of their substantial nature and magnitude, or because they are unequal in terms of their predominant function; yet,
even if they are unequal in terms of their shape and dimension, the earth element is still perceivable.
Regarding the other three great elements whose magnitude is so small as to be imperceptible yet are nonetheless real:
if those three possessed distinct magnitudes,
their respective sizes should be perceivable, because they would possess differentiated dimensions.
Since even a small portion cannot be found, it is known that there is no "greatness of three" herein.
You say:
"In your own school, there is no inequality regarding greatness within a stone."
Because they do not exist even in part,
like flowers in the sky.

If it is argued that while the element of earth has a functional utility and its characteristics can be perceived, the other three great elements lack such utility and thus cannot be perceived— [this is not so].
To claim that function depends upon a substance,
when that substance does not exist while the function does,
is an irrational adherence.
The Pramāṇa states:
"Within a stone, there is definitively no capacity for water and so forth,
because it lacks their essential nature."
Like the horns of a rabbit and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the production from seeds," Jing says:
This means that all forms arise from their respective seeds of form within the ālayavijñāna;
by virtue of possessing their own seeds,
they undergo transformation and arise upon encountering conditions.
Just as water becomes ice when cold and thus constitutes earth,
and as water encounters fire and thus becomes flowing moisture and constitutes water—
when it is said that although there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) through such processes, there nonetheless exist their respective elements (dhātu) and so forth.
Previously, we refuted the Lesser Vehicle’s claim regarding the existence of water and fire within that stone;
now, we clarify that within the solid stone, there exist the respective elements (dhātu) for the seeds of water, fire, and so forth.
Therefore, there is no error.
Tai [Zhi] says:
"The previous treatise discusses the two types of 'great': namely, the Great [Vehicle] itself and its creation."
Regarding this, why is it not stated that one great element (mahābhūta) which can produce both faculties (indriya) and objects (viṣaya) maintains three types [of seeds]?
The explanation is:

Now, regarding what is called "seed" (*bīja*): it is only within the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) that there exists that which can produce the other elements, such as the great elements themselves; therefore, it is called a "seed.
For this reason, within the eye, there are no seeds for other sense organs.

Second is the gate of the true principle:

The three types of moistening are neither identical nor different from the practice.
Based on the third, the nature of firmness, there are the seeds of impure moisture;

Alternatively, it may be explained solely on the basis of the principle of concomitant transformation.

There are three ways in which momentum induces the intermediate state (*antarābhava*):

Regarding the "desire for requisites" (kāma) of the three heavens of the six classes of gods and the northern continent (Uttarakuru), Jing says:

They are produced by the power of mental intention (*āśaya*).
On the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*), garments, musical instruments, and other such objects grow upon trees;

The tree then bends its branches so that he may reach out his hand and take it;

Therefore, there is no fault. Ji said:
"All of these arise from karma."

The meaning is this:

If one asks who does not say that its fruit arises from karma, [the answer is] none; however,
this statement is made based on the predominant perception of what is present before one,
and thus it says, "it arises from desire."
Regarding the latter two types of arising:
because they are sustained by water, sprouts and so forth are able to arise;
this is called "arising through sustenance."
Conversely, when the sun, fire,
and so forth cause the sprout to wither and dry up,
this is called "reductive arising" (*apacaya-utpāda*).
From here below is the second section, clarifying the harmonious mixture and non-separation [of the elements].
Jing says:

It arises in this manner due to the dominant causal power of those respective seeds, because it functions as that which possesses roots.
Such is the reason.

Because these [elements] exist within the aggregate,

This clarifies that they are blended together and not separate from one another.

although the textual characteristics are as they are now...

That is to say, by virtue of being struck or touched by the earth element,

as the Tripiṭaka Master says,

Regarding "by means of superior meditative concentration" (*samādhi*), etc.:
Just as when one cultivates the divine eye and ear faculties by entering the superior concentration of the first dhyāna,
