The Master [Xuanzang] said: "The three meanings, such as transformation (pariṇāma),
are to be correlated with the five meanings— arising (utpatti), dependence (niśraya), establishment (pratiṣṭhā), maintenance (dhṛti), and sustenance (upastambha)— as explained below."
Among these, the transformation of the evolving being involves three types of causes: the generative cause, the supporting cause, and the nourishing cause.
Specifically, the preceding primary elements (mahābhūtas) act as the generative cause, while the subsequent [elements] that follow according to karma act as the supporting cause.
The power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) should be understood as one portion of the cause of nourishment (*puṣṭi-hetu*).
The remaining [factors] constitute the cause of establishment (*vyavasthāna-hetu*).
Sustenance (*dhṛti*) is the cause of maintenance (*dhṛti-hetu*).

In the third fascicle of this *Mūla-bhūmi*, there is further extensive clarification of the five causes and an explanation of the meaning of "greatly produced" (*mahābhautika*); these are the four interpretations.
Regarding the phrase "by the power of superior concentration" (*adhipati-samādhi-balāt*), according to Master Tai:
The preceding statement says: "If one follows this [view], that which is bound by these [elements] is produced from the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound by those same [realms].
If one discusses production from the great elements in terms of retribution (vipāka), it pertains exclusively to the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
If one discusses it in terms of meditative concentration (samādhi), they likewise transform into the great elements," as stated in the text of this passage.
It is like the "fruition-form" (*vipākaja-rūpa*) that arises when one emerges from an immaterial-sphere absorption (*ārūpya-samāpatti*);
because this arisen form is a transformation of the immaterial-sphere absorption,
it follows the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) and is bound to the immaterial realm.
This derived matter is bound according to the meditative absorption;
it is also bound to the formless realm.
The preceding text [refers to] both of the upper two realms.

Now, within this meditative concentration, the primary elements (mahābhūta) that first arise in the initial moment exist only as solidity, moisture, heat, and motion, and do not yet serve as the basis for derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
It is only in subsequent moments that they then become the basis for derived matter.
How is this known?

It is because the text below in this very fascicle states that the matter which is the fruit of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not depend on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), but depends solely upon meditative concentration;
yet, by way of its category, the image (*pratibimba*) of samādhi is also termed "derived from the primary elements" (*mahābhūta-nirmita*).
The meaning of the text here is as follows:
if one considers them in terms of being associated with the same mental moment,
it is like the principle of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) being equal in their maturation (vipāka) across different realms.
When there are primary elements (mahābhūta) at the outset,

there are derived forms (upādāyarūpa). These are called "not dependent on primary elements" if they are of the same category as the primary elements of the preceding moment of the aforementioned three samādhis.
Therefore, it is also designated as "derived from the four great elements.
If it were not a form such as meditative concentration (samādhi) and the like,
the great elements and the derived matter would necessarily be produced simultaneously.
The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of this meditative concentration are produced at a different time;

as for the statement in this text that "the primary elements arise first," it means that the preceding moment transforms into the primary elements, and only in the subsequent moment are the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced.
It is not that they are created simultaneously with the thought;
rather, because they arise based upon that [thought], they are said to be "created.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Another interpretation is this:
here, based on the fact that the actual matter (*dravya-rūpa*) is the fruit of meditative concentration, it is therefore transformed into the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within that concentration.

However, according to the subsequent passage, where it is stated that they are not transformed into the primary elements, this refers to the provisional matter (*prajñapti-rūpa*), which must depend upon the actual primary elements for its construction.
Therefore, it is taken that the form of the image belonging to the category of the previously defined samādhi is produced from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Since it is stated to be "the image belonging to the category of samādhi," this interpretation is not as [previously] suggested.
Furthermore, in this context, according to the actual reality, all determinate matter (*niyata-rūpa*) is transformed into the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

In the subsequent passage, it is explained that one must rely upon the fundamental substance (*mūla-dravya*) for there to be a determination of the transformation into the great primary elements within the intermediate state.
Therefore, within the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), the primary elements (mahābhūta) are not discussed or mentioned as being "derived from the great" (upādāya),
because they are the fundamental conditions; nevertheless,
they may still be designated as "derived from the great."
Now, referring back to the previous fascicle, it states that "one attains mastery over all forms and can transform them into the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
This text serves as proof,
just as the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*) induces the great elements and so forth.
This passage refers to the matter produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within meditative concentration.
If the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) does not induce the primary elements but induces only the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
the subsequent text states that it is not "produced by the primary elements," because it is said to be "produced" in reference to its arising from the samādhi of the reflected image (*pratibimba*).
The sixty-sixth [fascicle] states: "One obtains those elements (dhātu) and those primary elements (mahābhūta) accordingly.
Cè says: "That which is produced by karma."
The preceding section clarified the principle of the sequential arising of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Due to the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of karma and the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-kāya-bīja*),
at the moment of initial conception, the earth element arises first to construct the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) as well as the eye and other faculties.
Due to this great power, it is only at the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that the four faculties, such as the eye,
are finally produced. Fourth, it clarifies how the fruit undergoes transformation due to five conditions,
just like the cultivation of grain crops.
When water and manure are applied in harmony and supplemented by human ingenuity,
the resulting fruit will be superior.
Once they encounter conditions such as wind and frost,
the fruits all suffer from a disease of their nature;
their color and flavor undergo transformation.
This is called the power of the great elements.
Second, by means of human effort in cultivation,
the fruit is free from remote evil.
This is called the power of a person's causal strength.
Third, it is by means of incantations;
for example, one may cast a spell upon a forest of trees to cause them to wither and die.
There are non-Buddhists skilled in incantations who,
through their spells, cause withered fruit to grow;
fourth, by means of supernatural powers, they effect transformations.
They may transform good into evil,
or transform evil into good;
in five ways, they rely upon the human species as the basis for the maturation of their prior karma.
The fruit follows through transformation.
Fifth, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is established. Two.

First, it is clarified that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises with the seeds of names and phrases as its cause and the perfuming of the constituent parts (*bhāgīya-vāsanā*) as its condition.
Next, the reason for its existence is established through a series of questions and answers.
Jing says:
The opponent raises an objection, saying:
"What need is there for an intermediate state (antarābhava) when one dies here and is reborn there?
It is like a person who, upon reaching a precipice, calls out and an echo immediately arises."
Could it be that there is some other entity which transmits that sound to the valley so that an echo arises?
The Master’s intended answer is that the echo itself is indeterminate.
Just as when one calls out toward a valley,
an echo emerges in response according to the size of the call,
so too is it only my own delusion.
The existence at birth from the existence at death is not like this.
Furthermore, it is difficult [to explain],
just as the reflection of the moon in the heavens appears in water.
Could it be that some substance must transmit this reflection?
Now the Master of the Treatise refutes this:
the moon in the heavens does not perish, yet the reflection in the water arises.
Once the existence at death has ceased, the existence at birth begins;
therefore, they are not identical.
Furthermore, the opponent says:
For example, when a person’s mind takes an object in another location as its focus,
at that time, could there possibly be some distinct entity that transmits the mind to that other location?
The Master of the Treatise refutes this by saying:
Nor should it be said that, just as one grasps an object of perception, there is no movement toward it; for example,
when a person directs their mind toward another place,
it is merely a remote mental apprehension, and the mind does not physically travel there.
The mind that takes birth must necessarily proceed there.
K’i says:
"In the Mahāyāna, echoes are like shadows."
When heard by the ear, one hears only the original sound;
it is merely because the mind is deluded that one says there is an echo within the valley.
It is similar to an image in a mirror.
Now, proceeding according to that school,
it is said that [the entity] does not perish.
This is the fourth section among the ten gates, clarifying its formal establishment.
It consists of eight sections.
The first states: "One should know that the primary elements (mahābhūta) first occupy a location, and subsequently the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) arises in dependence upon this location.
This is stated according to the gate of the supported and the support.
Because at the time when karma produces its retribution, it arises with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its support,
there is simultaneously the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*);
for derived matter is that which depends [upon the primary elements].
Therefore it is said that other derived forms (upādāya-rūpa) function depending on this location;
they do not exist at a different time.
When the earth-element (pṛthivī-dhātu) arises as an obstruction, [the others follow].
The great elements of other stages cannot arise again;
they are designated as "great elements" because derivative matter (bhautika-rūpa) arises in dependence upon them.
They do not pervade [the locus] at different times.
Because the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is supported by those predominant primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it possesses resistance;
thus, other primary elements cannot produce further derived matter.
Second, the coarse and subtle nature of the four great elements is explained.
If the seeds of the earth and the fruits produced from the earth are both superior in essence and function, they are coarse;
the other two [realms] are progressively more subtle. Third, it is explained that the substance of sound is intermittent, arising instantaneously like light.
Tai said:
"It is attached to the Great Creator.
He further explained:
Regarding "sounds external to matter":
these are merely the great elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa) external to matter.
Master Ji says:
According to this passage,
sound is identical to the light of a lamp;
it is separated from its substance and consists of the four great elements, specifically the element of wind.
The winds that circulate in all the spheres and are called "constantly continuous" include the wind that supports the solar and lunar disks, named Vairambha,
as well as the wind-circles (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) and so forth.
It is called "constant continuity.
Regarding those who act upon things, it is called "constant appropriation.
Jing said:
Just as the winds within the various channels of the human body move constantly without ceasing,
it is called "perpetual sustenance" (*nitya-parigraha*).
Tai [Shi] said:
The wind element maintains objects so that they do not disperse;
this is called "constant gathering.
Master Ji says:
Holding objects so that they do not scatter is called "constant gathering.
This differs from the third fascicle of the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Holding together by means of a mechanical device is called "constant continuity."
Jingyun: Water-mills are renamed "mechanisms" (jiguān);
they draw wind by means of water.
The wind-force causes it to turn,
moving continuously in succession.
Tai says:
It is the wind of the joints and bones. Ce says:
It is the wind of the inhalation and exhalation within the bodies of sentient beings.
Fifth is the element of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"According to this, the element of space consists of light and darkness as its color."
Jingyun: According to the Western tradition,

the form of the space-element (ākāśa-dhātu-rūpa) is merely a provisional designation established upon the portion manifested when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes great empty space as its object.
Regarding "eternal darkness and light":
the dwelling place between the two worlds is eternally dark,
while the various devas are eternally bright.
Regarding the statement, "One should know that this also depends upon a collection of matter (rūpa-kalāpa)":
Jing says,
"This refers to the matter of the space-element (ākāśa-dhātu)."
This means it manifests based on the periphery of accumulated matter;
that is, based on things such as houses, kilns, and walls. Ki says:
As it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa*, "it is called 'color adjacent to ākāśa' (ākāśānantarika-rūpa)";
*ākāśa* is ultimate resistance (*parama-pratighāta*),
and this color is adjacent to it.
In this context, based upon the locations of sound, visible form, and so forth, there exists the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) within those locations of visible form and so forth;
thus, the space-element consists of the provisional [designation] of visible forms such as the six types of long and so forth.
Although there is no accumulation of subtle [atoms],
there is an accumulation of coarse blue and so forth that forms a shape.
As for what is called the fault of confusion:
Because there is the fault that a single dharma would be both long and short;
furthermore, because cognitions such as those of a chariot and so forth are subject to destruction—
just as when one takes away the wheels and axle, the cognition of that "chariot" and so forth is lost.
Because they exist in mutual dependence.

Seventh, regarding the statement that "the form which is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) should be understood as having only visible color (*varṇa*), shape (*saṃsthāna*), and so forth":
this is because that practitioner originally grasps visible colors such as blue and yellow that exist outside of the concentration.
When one enters meditative absorption and observes an object, the appearing aspect (nimittabhāga) that resembles its essential nature (svabhāva) is called the "manifest color" (varṇanimitta).
Furthermore, although this color within concentration cannot be seen [by others],
it is called "manifest color" because, by taking it as a condition, it causes others to transform their own minds and perceive manifest color.
Regarding this, there are two explanations.
One states that the matter resulting from meditative concentration (samādhi-phala-rūpa) truly lacks fragrance and taste.
If that is so, why does the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Eight Liberations) state:
"As for 'superior,' it refers to blue, yellow, and so forth"?
If they are inferior, this refers to odors, tastes, and so forth.
The commentary states:
whenever one enumerates the factors inseparable from the objects of observation, [these are included].
The inferior [objects] are odor and flavor;
even when correctly contemplating, one contemplates only visible form.
If that concentrated mind were to contemplate odor or flavor, [it would not be concentration].
If that concentrated mind were to belong to a higher realm,
it would entail the fault of odors and tastes existing in that higher realm; therefore,
it is said that the causes for their arising are lacking there.
Furthermore, there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the higher realms;
this is because odors and tastes have no utility there.
Second, it is said:
Because of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is indeed possible to manifest [them].
Thus, the fifty-second fascicle states:
"By virtue of superior concentration, one attains mastery over all forms."
Furthermore, in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
it is said that a bodhisattva’s faculty of the nose perceives the fragrance of the palaces in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Although it is stated in this context that there are no odors or tastes there, [the bodhisattva nonetheless perceives them].
However, that which is transformed consists only of odors, tastes, and so forth, which belong to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
There is no impediment to taking the former interpretation as the basis.
Question:

Regarding the statement that "because the elements of odor and taste, as well as their functions, are absent in the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is no odor, taste, and so forth": if that were the case,
then since the seeds of the primary elements (mahābhūta) would likewise be absent in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they should not transform into the primary elements and so forth.
Answer:
In the formless realm there is no matter consisting of karma,
yet there exists untainted great-element matter.
Therefore, there is form.
Since the realm of form lacks the retribution of odor and taste,
it likewise lacks the untainted seeds of odor and taste.
He asked again:
"If the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack retribution (*vipāka*), they nevertheless possess untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*).
Although the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) lacks the retribution of odors and tastes, what prevents it from possessing untainted seeds?"
The commentary explains:
Because the great elements (mahābhūta) of the formless realm have a functional utility,
even though they lack karmic retribution (vipāka), there nonetheless exist untainted (anāsrava) great elements.
Because odors and tastes serve no purpose in the form realm, they do not exist there as uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Tai says:
"Since the higher realms lack karma that draws forth edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), the nose and tongue faculties are not acquired."
Therefore, for them, odors and tastes lack the cause for karmic birth, as well as the function of the olfactory and gustatory faculties in apprehending their respective objects.
Cè (Cè) says: [as follows].
Although the mind in meditative concentration manifests the images of the five sense objects,
these belong to the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) and are not called "odor" or "taste.
They are only metaphorically designated as "odor" or "taste" because they resemble those respective objects.
Why is this? Because the higher dhyānas are definitely not causes for odor and flavor,
and because odor and flavor are also not utilized by the concentrated mind.

Regarding the statement, "The wind moving through space lacks co-emergent fragrance and so forth," this extended causal explanation clarifies that the wind moving through space lacks any fundamental, co-emergent fragrance and possesses only a conventional designation.
It is like when the wind encounters a flower;
the fragrance follows the wind and comes.
Question:
There would likewise be no tangible object (spraṣṭavya). Answer:
This tangible object fundamentally depends upon the wind element (vāyudhātu) and so forth.
Therefore, it is not analogous to external light.
Regarding the two explanations in the *Śāstra*, one says:
Within the radiance of the sun, there are only the great elements (mahābhūta) of luminous color;
all other particles are entirely absent.
This is one explanation.
Only the touch of the great mass of fire and its radiance exist;
since all else is absent,
it is said to be unobtainable.
Furthermore, regarding the external [halo] being identical in meaning to the *Tattvasiddhi*, Jing said:
"The light outside the wheel lacks the great elements (*mahābhūta*) capable of creating it, as well as fragrance and so forth.
Master Tai has two explanations.
One interpretation is that there are derived forms (bhautika-rūpa) that are separated from their primary substance (upādāna-rūpa),
such as the light of the solar orb, which is derived from the great elements (mahābhūta) of the orb itself at a distance.
There is no magnitude in that which is not co-spatial;
this textual passage serves as proof for its status as the "supporting cause" (*dhṛti-hetu*) among the five causes.
This refers to the primary elements (mahābhūta) as the substance;
there are two interpretations.
Furthermore, there are also derived elements (bhautika), such as light.
Regarding the statement that "the great elements also separately produce light and so forth":
however, because fire is taken as a condition from within the fundamental wheel, it induces something subtle that cannot be perceived;
it is for this reason that it is said here to be non-existent.
Just as light surely possesses the tactile quality of heat,
though the term "heat" is used metaphorically,
it takes fire and water as its substance.
How could there be the sensation of heat arising apart from fire? Therefore, we know that it also possesses radiance.
As for the sensation of heat within the sun, it is simply the heat of the warm and hot portion of the fire within the solar orb.
It is not the fire element (*tejomahābhūta*) that produces light and color.
Sound should be understood according to this principle.
Master Ji says:
This contradicts the "supporting cause" (*dhṛti-hetu*) among the five causes,
for that [cause] is defined by the non-destruction of equal measure.
Question:
Why are there no odors or tastes?
Because odors and tastes are subtle, they do not exist within light;
whereas form and tangibility are coarse, they are present within light as well.
If heavy existence were tangible,
it should exist within the light of the fire element;
why then do you say it does not?
Now, when it is said that there is no light produced,
it does not mean that there is no heat from the sun during midday. Likewise,
one might also say that fragrance is light and has nothing with which it coalesces, just as light does.
Is there also a fragrant portion from the solar orb that reaches far away?
He replied:
Because it is light, as previously explained, it remains until it is exhausted.
Another interpretation is that while the sensation of heat exists, the other three great elements are said to be absent; it is not, however,
that the fire element itself is also absent.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that the matter which is the fruit of superior meditative concentration (samādhi) depends solely on superior concentration and not on the primary elements (mahābhūta),
Jing says:
"The matter of mastery in concentration is not produced by the four great elements."

However, as for the previous statement that "those very [elements] are derived from the great elements," this is said based on the fact that those primary elements (mahābhūta) and the determined matter (niyata-rūpa) share the same basis and arise simultaneously; thus, it is called "derived from the great elements.
For example, when the mind of the first dhyāna contemplates the determined matter of the dhyāna, it immediately induces and nurtures the primary elements.
The same applies to those bound by the first dhyāna arising simultaneously.

For example, when one takes up a blue seat while in a distracted state as a preliminary means, and from this enters meditative absorption to perform the contemplation of blue color, manifesting a blue image, this is called "the color of concentration," just like taking up the blue seat.

By means of this meditative concentration, one contemplates that the color previously seen—such as the blue quality of a sitting mat—is produced from and dependent upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that sitting mat.
Ji (基) says:
"This refers exclusively to the contemplation of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)."
Since there is no expectation of observing the great elements [within it],
that which remains unchanged within meditative concentration does not become the great elements;
yet, because it is described as being derived from the substantial matter of the image prior to concentration, it is likewise designated as "derived from the great elements."
The previous argument was based on the theory that the mind transforms the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) during the period of deliberation;
therefore, it was held that even the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) within meditative concentration is transformed into the primary elements. This is not the case here.
Therefore, there is a distinction.
Question:
Regarding the intention directed toward the future, within the Great Contemplation (*mahā-vipaśyanā*), the great elements (*mahā-bhūta*) do not exist.
Qixin asks: "In the contemplation of non-creation, is there no created matter, but only the great elements?
Therefore, we know that adopting the former interpretation is superior. Cè says:
Previously, it was stated that they are "of the same bond" (*sabandhana*) because they are large as categorized under the *dharmāyatana* derived from the mental concomitants;
now, however, it is based on the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in relation to the distant object of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
The eighth [point] clarifies that among the various types of matter, there are those that are visible and resistant;
the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) possesses both the qualities of being invisible and non-resistant.
While it may be so that in the Hīnayāna the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) contains only non-informative matter (avijñaptirūpa),
in this Mahāyāna, as previously stated, the sphere of phenomena contains actual matter that constitutes the enjoyment of others.
Why is this invisible and non-obstructive?
Because the matter transformed from the concentrated mind is actually subtle; it does not occupy a specific location and is not produced by karma, and therefore it is non-obstructive.
The matter and so forth of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) do not serve as a precedent, as they all depend upon a specific location.
In this context, if it is for the enjoyment of another, then that which is seen by the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) should be subsumed under the sense-base of matter (*rūpāyatana*).
Why, then, is it called the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
The meaning is this:
because from the moment of its original arising, it is produced by a concentrated mind, it is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects.
Although one may see others using [the Dharma] for other purposes, one does not expect such persons to be vessels for the Dharma.
This is the fifth section of the Ten Gates, which explains the meaning of the "streams" (srotas);
it specifically resolves the meaning of the three types of streams as presented in the third fascicle of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
Master Ji says:
"Regarding the statement that the first, the outflowing [result], further has four kinds,
the first two among these are..."
It is not separate from the two types previously mentioned— maturation and nourishment—
and is thus a single entity;
its intrinsic nature is that of outflow.

According to the following passage, excluding the matter of the sense organs (*indriya-rūpa*), the remaining three types of outflow (*niṣyanda*)—the luminous and the selected—are also characterized by an intrinsic nature of outflow;
their characteristics are easily understood.

Thus, it is only the five external objects (*viṣaya*) that are exclusively outflows. Among the five organs, both the primary (*maula*) and the nurtured (*aupacayika*) are subject to transformation and decay (*vipariṇāmadharman*), and they may also be considered the second type of outflow.
The two types of outflow (*niṣyanda*) are the pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and the ripening (*vipāka*), and so forth.
The cessation of the preceding moment and the arising of the subsequent moment is called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*).

Within this, the internal faculties and so forth, which obtain the names of "ripening" (*vipāka*) and "nourishment" (*aupacayika*), are termed "the rest," while external objects are [also included therein].
There are only two streams: the stream of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and the stream of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Regarding the stream of transformation, its meaning extends by analogy to the three types: the fundamental nature, retribution (*vipāka*), and sustenance (*poṣaṇa*).
The first, at the moment of its initial arising, is called the stream of maturation (*vipāka-srotas*).
From the second moment onward, the continuity of the maturation (*vipāka*) flows; this includes both nominal and substantial maturation.
As for substantial maturation:
from the first moment of the *ālaya-vijñāna* until the end of life, its very essence is maturation.
It may also be called "born of maturation" because it arises from the preceding and succeeding moments of maturation;
this very passage reconciles [the two views],
for maturation is initially predominant, and thus it is named after that first moment.

This is not as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts, which say that the ālayavijñāna is the actual maturation (*vipāka*), whereas the others are called "maturation" only metaphorically because they arise from maturation;
for now, the eighth consciousness may also be designated as "arising from maturation" (*vipākaja*).
However, within the conventional sense of maturation (*vipāka*), according to this text, it may also be termed "maturation.
Because it is the very first moment of the maturation produced by karma, it is conventionally designated as "maturation";
the second moment and those following are likewise termed "arising" (*jāti*).
The remainder is as explained in the third *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Regarding the "pervasive abiding" (*sthāna-vyāpin*) within the flow of nourishment:
because it possesses a continuous lineage (*saṃtati*), it is called "pervasively abiding."
The intensification of the characteristics refers to the increase of their substance.
It should be understood that the remaining types of nourishment—the flow [of nutriment]—also arise by means of food; that is, the aforementioned food.
Since it is the basis for those [other nourishments], they consist of sleep and the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
That which arises from the cultivation of sublime attention (*manasikāra*) is concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that the various material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) undergo transmigration through two kinds of flow;
this refers to the flow that is naturally concordant (*nisyanda-nisyanda*).
Why are the internal faculties not considered *vipariṇāma-vipākaja* (resulting from transformation and maturation)?
Because when they are touched or struck, they undergo disintegration;
therefore, this is not mentioned here.
It may also be said:

to the question of why the *vipāka* (maturation) is not the *aupacayika* (accumulated), the answer is that because there exists a continuity of the accumulated which can encompass and sustain the *vipāka* and the *naiṣyandika* (outflowing), there is the appearance of growth and so forth.
Regarding the distinction between the nourishing stream (*aupacayika-srotas*) and the ripening stream (*vipāka-srotas*):
there is a separate nourishing stream, for the nourishing stream is not identical to the ripening stream.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "It is like external walls that defend an inner city."
Regarding the statement that "matter not comprised within the sense faculties should be known to possess three kinds of outflows"—
namely, those of maturation (*vipāka*), accumulation (*aupacayika*), and outflow (*naiṣyandika*)— the outflow of outflow is precisely the outflow of transformation (*vipariṇāma*).
There are also those that are of the nature of natural outflow (*nisyanda*).
Here, the general statement should be understood as follows:
internal bases that support the sense organs (*indriya-saṃniśrita*) consist of both maturation (*vipāka*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
External objects consist solely of their own nature as outflows (*niṣyanda*), lacking both maturation (*vipāka*) and nourishment (*aupacayika*), because they are not internal bodies;
thus it should be stated accordingly.
Here, the general term "all minds and mental factors" refers to those arising from outflows, maturation, and the second characteristic—the flow of intense nourishment (*aupacayika*).
In the preceding text, it was stated that the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is extensive and is nurtured by food,
as it is not mental.
Furthermore, among the various sound-elements (*śabdadhātu*), there are those that are results of maturation (*vipākaja*) which do not exist as sounds.
According to what Xuanzang said:
because the seeds of sound are constantly in a state of succession,
the sphere of sound (*śabdadhātu*) is a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
Because its active manifestation is intermittent and subject to cessation, it is not termed "maturation" (*vipāka*).
As the Master Jing says:
"The seven bases are called the 'retribution realm' (*vipākadhātu*); they are maturation."
Now, this cannot be so.
The seven parts being even and full constitute seven types of maturation (vipāka),
because among the twenty-two faculties (indriya), the seeds of all these faculties are indeed maturations.
In this context, sound should also be understood accordingly.
As the master Vasumitra previously explained regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*), they are the causes; that is, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce sound.
These great elements are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), whereas the sound itself is not maturation-born.
This corresponds to the third transmission of sound,
as sound arises from retribution.
The sixth section of the Ten Gates clarifies karma.
First, the karma of the derived matter produced by the four great elements is explained;
next, the three distinct categories of objects perceived by the eyes and ears are explained;
finally, it is explained that motion based on a substratum differs from matter, yet is not distinct from that which does not differ [from it].
The preceding section has two parts:
first, a detailed explanation of the five specific functions of each of the four great elements;
second, a general explanation of the common functions shared by the four great elements.
Regarding the function of striking, breaking, and transforming the earth element:
it is like forging iron or striking a clay pot, and so forth.
As for its establishment:
It is established by depending on the derived matter of the earth element.
As for "depending," it means that the derived matter of the earth element is able to exist [thereby].
Regarding "karma that causes harm":
it is like harming sentient beings through a solid tactile sensation, rather than [harming] things such as crops. Regarding "karma that gathers":
[it refers to karma that accumulates results].
The earth element can sustain and benefit the derived matter;
when the wind element first arises,
it initiates its own activity through movement.
After the body has moved,
a further wind arises that causes it to move incessantly;
this is called the "concomitant" (anuvartaka) karma.
This generally clarifies the four great elements and the five types of action.
As it says in the first fascicle of the Abhidharma:
"It is called 'created' (kṛta) based on five causes."
The "cause of arising" (janakahetu) is the "cause of origination" (utpādakahetu);
that is to say, because matter does not arise apart from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
As for the causal basis,
it is the transformative cause;
that is to say, because the primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derived matter (upādāyarūpa) lack the capacity to occupy a distinct location once they have been relinquished.
The establishing cause is the conforming cause (*anuvartaka-hetu*),
due to the great transformation.
Because the derived matter undergoes transformation in accordance with it.
As for the "sustaining cause," this is the "abiding cause."
This means that because the various derived forms produced by the primary elements arise in a similar succession,
they are maintained and prevented from being interrupted.
As for the sustaining cause (puṣṭi-hetu):
This refers to the cause of growth;
that is to say, because the primary elements nourish those derived forms, causing them to increase.
Next, it is explained that the objects of the eye and ear are common to all three moral natures.
First is the volition of preparatory application,
which refers to the volition that arises from a distance with the intent to initiate this action.
Second is the volition of the certainty that one will definitely perform this action.
The three types of origination are:
origination as cause (*hetu-samutthāna*),
which is the mind arising in the immediately preceding moment.
Now, the subsequent accomplishment of good or evil necessarily depends on the motivating volition (*samutthāna-cetanā*).
Because this is a volition of superior grade, it conforms to its nature;
it does not depend on the volition of preparatory application (*prayoga-cetanā*) or the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*), which are of inferior or middling grades.
Furthermore, the first two categories of volition (cetanā) pertain to both the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Volition on the path of seeing constitutes an extremely remote preparatory application (dūre-prayoga) that is only capable of initiating karma;
this second category of superior volition, however, belongs to the path of cultivation.
If the volition that arises at each moment (*kṣaṇa*) also has this as its basis—
just as one obtains the precepts when entering the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*)— then in this case,
it is because [the action] is initiated by three types of volition.
Visible forms and sounds manifest as good or evil;
this refers to their manifestation as good or evil, not to their essence being good or evil.
Other objects, such as odors and tastes, are not prompted by these three types of volition.

It is like space and so forth.

When one moves the hand,

Your assertion that it does not cease contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The seventh section of the ten gates clarifies momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
It is divided into two parts:
first, it clarifies that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) possess momentary cessation.

The subsequent section clarifies that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the fruits of the mind; one should know that, like the mind itself, they are all momentary (*kṣaṇika*). The preceding section consists of three parts:

second, the refutation of externalist views by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); and third, [the conclusion].

Jing says:
This text refutes the tenets of the Sthavira school.
They claim that past and future phenomena do not exist, and that only the present exists;
furthermore, they maintain that there are only three categories of phenomena.
First, form; second, mind; third, mental factors.
Mind and mental factors arise with great rapidity.
In the present, it lasts for two moments,
namely arising and ceasing;
this refers to the preceding mind from its emergence until the phase of cessation.
The final mind has already reached the stage of arising;
the third mind arises at the stage of the characteristic of arising,
while that second mind has already reached the stage of the characteristic of cessation.
Matter-dharmas are sluggish;
therefore, they persist in the present for three moments, namely:
arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Now, this argument is refuted.
Ji says: "This cites the correct principle, stating that [dharmas] cease spontaneously."
This differs from the Saṃmitīya school and others.
They posit that at the time of initial birth, the internal body, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
and so forth are called "arising," while at the time of subsequent death, they are called "ceasing."
They dwell constantly therein.
When the world and so forth [re-emerge],
it is called the "birth" at the beginning of the kalpa.
The destruction of an eon (*kalpa*) is called "cessation.
Within that [period], the intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*) and so forth do not undergo arising and ceasing;
nevertheless, they also admit that things such as lamps and lightning, as well as the dharmas of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), all arise and cease moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*).
One immediately cites this matter commonly accepted by both parties as proof,
stating that it is "perceptibly obtainable.
One should then formulate the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
The thesis that the eye and other forms perish as soon as they arise has "being conditioned" as its reason,
with "the light of a lamp and so forth" as the example.
The lower [view] is not that which arises from the causes and conditions of false attachment;
it is like the Sarvāstivāda position that fire serves as the condition for the extinction of fuel,
yet it is actually the condition for the fuel’s persistence.
This is refuted herein.
One should not claim that the cause which produces is identical to the cause which destroys, because their characteristics are different.
Jing says:
As stated in the *Dṛṣṭānta-paryāya*:
"The arising of phenomena has a cause;
the cessation of phenomena has no cause."
Taking the meaning of the Mahāyāna, it is stated thus:
The Abhidharmikas maintain that cessation has a cause.
Question:
Just as when an arrow is shot into the air, its departure can be said to have a cause because force is exerted;
but when it falls, no force is exerted—what then serves as its cause?
To this, he replies: when the arrow is traveling, it encounters obstructions such as shields, and it is precisely these that cause it to fall.
If there were no obstructing object, it would fall at the very moment force is applied to shoot it;
if it was not shot originally, by what means could it now fall?
By this principle.
Since all phenomena that arise and perish possess causes,
I shall now cite the doctrine of the Abhidharma to provide a formal refutation:
one should not claim that the cause of arising is identical to the cause of perishing, for their characteristics are distinct.
Since arising and ceasing are distinct, how can they share a single cause? Ji says:
"For example, the Sarvāstivāda school establishes through the principle of *pramāṇa* (inference) that cessation also has a cause."
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows:
"Cessation also has a cause" is the thesis (*pakṣa*);
"because it is conditioned" (*saṃskṛtatvāt*) is the reason (*hetu*).
It is like the analogy for the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, those of the Mahāyāna and the Sautrāntika school say: "If cessation were without a cause, it would follow that it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)," because it would lack a cause.
This is the reason.
"It is just like space.
This is a proof by negation (*pratiṣedhānumāna*).
Now, the Mahāyāna and other schools refute this, saying:
If you maintain that the characteristic of cessation has a cause, then your thesis— that it should cease again— follows,
because it possesses a cause;
this is just like the case of the characteristic of arising as an analogy.

Cessation does not arise from causes; [Reason: because it does not cease subsequently;

Furthermore, it is refuted as follows:

Because they possess causes and so forth, these are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
this is the reason, just as the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) serves as an illustration.

I now challenge you: your thesis that the two characteristics of arising and ceasing do not share a single cause must be accepted, because their characteristics are different.
Therefore, [your] reason is invalid.
For example, [the categories of] suffering and pleasure, or good and evil, or form and mind;
this single inference (*anumāna*) is precisely the formal inference (*sādhana-anumāna*) intended by the present text.
However, this inference suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Why is this? First, the Mahāyāna also admits that a single real characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-tattva*) serves as the cause for the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and likewise serves as the cause for the form (*rūpa*) transformed by itself.

The Hīnayāna also admits that this very same perception (*saṃjñā*) is real; it neither obstructs the arising of form nor obstructs the arising of the mind, such that this single cause is capable of producing both mind and form.
If that is so, are form and mind— despite their differing characteristics— caused by the same single cause, or are they—
as with the wholesome and the unwholesome— not caused by the same single cause due to their differing characteristics?

Furthermore, it must be stated that according to this explanation based on causes and conditions, for example, within the ālayavijñāna, a single seed of form can produce both the manifest form and its own corresponding seed; thus, one may say that the characteristics of form and the seed are also distinct.

However, since this single type [of cause] can produce both material and non-material phenomena, it is a causal condition for both; thus, there is also the fallacy of uncertainty (*anaikāntika*) regarding this.
Furthermore, one may also refute the two characteristics of arising and ceasing by means of inference (*anumāna*), as they share a single cause.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:

Your "destruction of that which possesses a cause" ought not to be the thesis of "destruction," because it arises from causes no different from those that produce [the entity]. This is the reason (*hetu*).
This should be further examined and refuted by means of the analogy of its arising. Furthermore,
regarding the statement that "once a phenomenon has arisen, no other cause for its continued endurance can be found":
Tai says:
"This refutes the Sarvāstivādins [here referred to as the Saṃmitīyas], because they hold that material phenomena (rūpadharma) endure for many moments.
The Master of the Treatise objects:
Since arising is itself cessation, a cause for abiding certainly does not exist.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
the various phenomena such as the eye have no cause for abiding because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like mental phenomena (*cittadharma*).
Master Ji said:
"If one were to argue that arising and ceasing are contradictory such that the cause of arising is not the cause of ceasing,
yet abiding and ceasing are not mutually exclusive such that the cause of abiding is itself the cause of ceasing."
Now, the refutation states:
Furthermore, if a phenomenon were to persist and wait for conditions of cessation before it could cease,
it would not cease spontaneously without depending on such conditions.
Since abiding has no cause,
how could it depend on conditions for cessation?
For it ceases spontaneously.
Therefore, one should know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not depend on external conditions for their cessation.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"The various forms, such as the eye and so forth, have no abiding other than momentary abiding; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*)."
Because it is conditioned and because it possesses arising and ceasing, it is a cause;
this is the original inference (*anumāna*).
Furthermore, one may also refute [the opponent] by means of another inference as follows:
The thesis that the eye and other forms do not endure for long is established because they are not included among those things that endure for long; this is the reason (*hetu*),
with lamps, lightning, and so forth serving as the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).
If it were to endure for a long time, it would necessarily be subsumed under the category of other things that endure for a long time,
just as space serves as a common analogy.
Furthermore, the proof states:
The thesis is that the various forms, such as the eye and so forth, lack a cause for long-term endurance.
The reason is that they are subsumed under one or another among [the categories of] the eye and the lamp and so forth.
The example is, for instance, like the lamp and so forth.
If it were to endure for a long time, it would certainly not be subsumed under any one of the categories such as the eye or a lamp, serving as a dissimilar example like space and so forth.
As for the claim that fire and the like must be the cause of destruction, that is unreasonable.
Jingyun: As an outsider might object, saying that we currently observe that things arising in accordance with the Dharma must necessarily depend upon causes and conditions.
If the conditions are not complete, a phenomenon cannot arise.
If cessation were dependent on causes, then if those causes were incomplete, the phenomenon should not cease; since this fault would follow, the cessation of phenomena is without cause.
This argument is not tenable.
We observe directly that fire and other factors destroy fuel;
is it not the case, then, that fire and the like serve as causes for destruction?
As for the claim that the Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu] asserts that the cessation of phenomena is causeless:
this current adherence to such a view is not reasonable.
Jñānagarbha says:
The Sarvāstivādins argue that fire is the cause of extinction;
therefore, the present refutation states: since this fire and the fuel arise and perish simultaneously, the fire cannot serve as the cause for the extinction of the fuel.
If fire and fuel arise simultaneously, then fire is not the cause of its own arising.
Since it perishes simultaneously with the fuel, how could it serve as the cause for its cessation?
If you claim that fire is the cause for its own cessation, [then...]
Since fuel and fire arise simultaneously, it would follow that as soon as they arise, the fuel must perish.
Yet we observe that fuel serves as the support for fire, and fire cannot extinguish it;
how, then, can fire be considered the cause for the extinction of the fuel?
An objection is raised: If that is so,
what further function does fire perform with respect to the fuel?
Furthermore, what prevents that which arises and ceases simultaneously from acting as a cause?
Now, it is said that only that which can serve as a condition for the arising of a subsequent, transformed phenomenon is described as the function of fuel.
The function of fuel is not for the purpose of extinguishing conditions;
as stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it is similar to light, snow, and vinegar.
They are largely the same.
Question:
If fire were not the cause of its own extinction,
would the fuel upon which this very fire depends still be called "fuel"?
Is it that from the very beginning, that which is designated as "fire" is also designated as "fuel"?
If it is also designated as fuel,
then as long as the fuel has not yet undergone transformation, it may still be called fuel.
Since it has already been transformed by fire,
it is different from what it was before;
it should not be called "fuel."
How can it be said that fire and fuel arise together and perish together?
If "fuel" is taken in its primary sense,
this refers to the wood that is being burned.
Since it is not actually fuel,
how can you say that fire serves as the condition for the transformation of that [fuel]?

If you claim that the fire of the first moment acts only as a condition for the transformation of subsequent moments and does not act as a condition for the transformation of the basis of the first moment, [then this is untenable].
If that were so, the fire of the first moment should not burn the fuel,
and the embers of subsequent moments should constantly produce fire.
Because the substratum is not the fuel itself.
Answer:
Herein, the outsider [argues] based on what is commonly known by worldly people that fire, which is capable of burning fuel, serves as the cause for its extinction.
Now, the author of the treatise again uses fire as it is commonly known to provide an explanation:
just as people in the world all know that one takes fire from elsewhere to burn that fuel.
The Master of the Treatise says: Fire burning fuel can only serve as the cause for the transformation of that fuel. Why?
Because, as is commonly known by the world, when fuel exists, fire exists.
That is to say, it arises simultaneously with the fuel;
since the fuel is absent, the fire is absent,
whereby it is known that it ceases simultaneously with the fuel.
Furthermore, it is commonly known among people of the world that firewood undergoes the transformation into ashes and embers due to fire.
The Master [Vasubandhu] merely employs conventional reasoning to address this objection;
however, if one were to rely on the ultimate reality of the Mahāyāna:
Phenomena such as fire perish as soon as they arise;
there is no such thing as this fire being able to burn that object.

Rather, it is due to external fire acting as a condition that it triggers within one's own mind the appearance of being burned and undergoing transformation. At the very moment immediately following the first instant of fire, consciousness transforms into the appearance of being burned.
One must not say that because the fire of the first moment serves as a condition, it acts as the productive condition for the transformation of the subsequent moment.
Furthermore, the claim that destruction itself is the cause of destruction is unreasonable, and so forth.
Jingyun: The outsider offers a rebuttal, saying:

In our school, there exists a distinct characteristic of cessation that is neither matter nor mind, which is capable of extinguishing all phenomena;

In your school, the characteristic of cessation coexists with the characteristic of arising.
The principle that the characteristic of arising gives rise to phenomena and the characteristic of cessation causes phenomena to cease is not established.
If he should attempt to rescue his position by claiming that,

If one were to claim that the shortest duration of a moment established by me is such that arising and ceasing must function simultaneously, [it would follow that they are not distinct].
When the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) of a future dharma is currently arising, that which is subject to cessation should then cease. If this were so,

Master Ji says:

Among the four characteristics established [for conditioned phenomena], the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is the cause for the cessation of form and the other aggregates.

cessation cannot be the cause for the cessation of form and so forth; therefore,

The *Pramāṇa* states:
"The thesis that future [phenomena] associated with cessation will have functional utility is established by the reason that you admit they already possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
It is like the analogy for the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
Question:
If your unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) also already possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), what function does it have?
This [entity] already possesses both essence and function.
Is it like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), which possess essence but lack function?
Or is it like the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), which possesses essence and thus immediately possesses function?
The commentary states:
The Sarvāstivādins establish the designations of the three time periods;
however, their own system does not include unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) within those [time periods].
Why is this? Because the designation "future" already exists,
and the designation "present" currently exists.
The name [of a phenomenon] from past lives still exists;
however, by merely stating that it "exists," its essence and function are already distinguished from being non-existent, as they are not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, one cannot take the unconditioned as a fallacy of "indefiniteness" (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, one cannot use a present phenomenon as an instance of the fallacy of "indefiniteness" (anaikāntika).
Moreover, one should formulate the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
Your thesis that the future birth-associated [phenomena] ought to be useless is [untenable].
Because it is subsumed within the future, it is a reason (*hetu*),
just as the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) serves as an illustration.
This inference and the previous inference may both employ their respective reasons interchangeably.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the nature of the characteristic of cessation is itself a phenomenon subject to disintegration and yet can cause all phenomena to cease of their own accord.

If one were to defend this by claiming that while the destruction and cessation of phenomena is merely non-existence, the characteristic of cessation itself exists as a distinct entity, [this would be untenable].
It is unreasonable that cessation exists separately outside of those phenomena, for such a thing cannot be found. If one were to offer a separate defense,
claiming that there is a distinct cessation whose nature is smaller than the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*),
[we reply that] apart from that great phenomenon characterized by cessation, no further small cessation possessing a nature of destruction can be found.
Therefore, this is not logical.
Furthermore,
it is explained that all phenomena perish spontaneously of their own accord and possess no distinct characteristic of cessation.
To claim that there is a characteristic of cessation existing separately outside of phenomena is ultimately untenable; therefore,
it is not logical, and the former interpretation is superior.
Regarding the statement, "If it is claimed that fire and so forth act as auxiliary companions for cessation in order to bring about extinction," Jing says:
The opponent further states that fire and so forth serve as auxiliaries for cessation.
The characteristic of extinction is that which is currently undergoing extinction.

If it is claimed that while the characteristic of extinction of the fuel and so forth is currently undergoing extinction, fire acts as an auxiliary to that extinction, [this is untenable].

"The causal capacities for the arising of various phenomena are distinct,

thus, the current [objection] is refuted.
If it is argued that there are distinct and individual capacities for producing those [effects], [we reply:]...
Since this distinction cannot be apprehended,
it is not logical. One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
When fuel and so forth are extinguished, they do not require the assistance of fire,
because the nature of their extinction is identical;
it is just like a lamp or a flash of lightning.

If it is claimed that fire acts as an auxiliary cause for destruction and that the characteristic of destruction (vināśalakṣaṇa) performs the actual destruction— such that both of these possess the capacity for destruction regarding a single piece of fuel—

If fire assists in the cessation of that fuel,
the characteristic of cessation brings about its actual cessation.
Because the fuel can be extinguished,
it is said that both components possess the capacity for extinction.
Furthermore, this fire lacks both the primary extinction and the characteristic of extinction.
Just as fire that assists in the extinction of fuel should not itself be extinguished,
it is therefore said that there is the fault of "having no functional capacity. Ki says:
By means of the two types— the characteristic of cessation and fire— and so forth,
all are conditions for cessation when compared to dharmas;
fire serves as an analogy for the characteristic of cessation.
It should correctly constitute the cause for cessation;
taking the characteristic of cessation as an analogy for fire,
it should correctly assist as the condition for cessation.
This is because both are conditions for the cessation of phenomena.
Since both types are thus untenable,
it is known that fire and the like cannot serve as auxiliary causes for cessation, nor can they constitute the primary cause of cessation.

which may be known by analogy with the four preceding lines.
Thus far has been clarified the meaning of the momentary destruction of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
The following clarifies that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), like the mind itself, perish moment by moment.
According to the correct principle,
all conditioned phenomena are the objective images (*nimittabhāga*) of the mind.

now, following Jing’s commentary,

First, regarding the basis:
the sentient world is the basis for demerit and merit,
while the receptacle world is the basis for their abode.
Sthiramati says:
"That which is real refers to the clear manifestation of blue and so forth;
that which is unreal refers to length and so forth, which are conventional designations and thus not clearly manifest."
From the phrase "by how many causes and conditions" onwards,
the text provides a detailed explanation in successive order.
First, it explains the non-destruction of the faculties.
That is to say, it is due to two causes, such as debilitation and so forth,

Furthermore, briefly stated, the transformation of the faculties and so forth occurs due to four conditions.
That which is initially good and subsequently bad, or initially bad and subsequently good, is all termed "transformation.
The first arises due to external conditions, meaning that through the enjoyment and appropriation [of objects],
non-sentient transgressions or favorable environments benefit the five sense faculties.
Regarding the impairment of external objects:
this refers to the impairment of the five sense faculties caused by external insentient things or adverse conditions.
Alternatively, it refers to the benefit or harm produced by other beings.
Regarding this fruit: first, the two types of objects—favorable and unfavorable—of a single sentient being either impair or benefit the five faculties;
second, through internal conditions, the fetters such as greed arise and damage the five faculties, or alternatively, through meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the five faculties are nourished.
Third, by the power of karma, those five faculties undergo transformation midway through their course, such as being initially unfavorable and subsequently favorable.
Fourth, by the transformation of the physical basis itself;
that is to say, there is mutual variation in the strength or weakness of those faculties, whether they are of the nature of retribution (*vipāka*) or nurtured growth (*aupacayika*).
Regarding the distinctions among their own characteristics:
due to four causes and conditions, all six consciousnesses that have arisen are subsequently termed the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Here, however, we distinguish the mental faculty in relation to the mental consciousness; when it perishes, it is called "destroyed," and its non-perishing is the opposite.
Next, the explanation of whether the objects of perception are manifest or not manifest.
Within this,
first, the actual determination of the manifestation of objects.
Next, the distinctions are explained in relation to the six objects of practice,
followed by a concluding summary.
Regarding the first of these:
First the question is posed, followed by the answer.
Within the answer, there are three parts.
The first concerns the manifestation of objects in relation to the five sense faculties.
Next, it is discussed in relation to the divine eye;
subsequently, in relation to the wisdom eye.
Within the first of these, there are again three parts.
First, the objects of the eye are clarified;
next, those of the ear;
and finally, those of the remaining three faculties.
At the beginning, regarding the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*),
it is said that what is neither concealed nor obscured is called "manifest before one" (*pratyakṣa*).
Regarding the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), it is said that whether it be light or darkness, both are called "manifest before one."
One should know that if there is contact, it is also termed "manifestly present" (pratyakṣa).
However, if the fleshly eye (māṃsa-cakṣus) is in contact with its object, it is not termed "manifestly present.
The same should apply to darkness as well.
Because there is mist,
there is an obstruction that is not distant.
As stated in the third chapter of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, there are four kinds of obstructions.
Regarding the statement that it differs from the ear and other faculties in terms of its magnitude and location,
and that it is "present" whether near or far:
although it is said that both the proximate and the distant are termed "manifest," [the eye-faculty] is distinct from those others.

According to the range of the faculties of sight and hearing of ordinary beings of the three vehicles, whatever is within their field of vision or hearing—whether distant or near, and according to their respective capacities and locations—is termed "manifest before them" (*pratyakṣa*); thus they are also able to see at a distance.
Furthermore, even when an object is obscured by darkness, it is still termed "manifest before them" with respect to a single eye.
Jingyun says:
"When one eye is obscured by a cataract, the object of color appears before the unobscured eye as well.
Ji says: [as follows].
This refers to the eyes of bats, owls, and the like, which possess obstructions within them;
yet, as with objects seen through rock crystal, they are able to see because of the presence of light and other such factors.
Ce says:
"The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is able to see forms obstructed by darkness;
therefore, it is called 'one eye'."
"The noble eye of wisdom (prajñā-cakṣus) has all types of forms as its object.
Regarding this, Ki states:
"In this context, it is not the eye of wisdom among the five eyes."
This is the Dharma-eye among those five eyes.
Because the noble ones take wisdom as their guide,
it is called the noble wisdom-eye.
Next, regarding the differentiation explained in contrast to the six [objects]:
as for "the five [objects], such as form, etc., being comprised within the three natures," the five sensory objects, such as form, do not transcend the three natures.
Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate;
form and sound—
some of these possess the nature of karma.
Therefore, there is functional activity;
however, the natures of odor, taste, and tangibility are not karma,
and they all lack functional activity.
The following explains the attention that gives rise [to concentration].
In the third *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is stated that the correct arising of attention is due to four causes:
the power of desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and so forth.
The tenth of the ten gates clarifies the gate of detachment.
Jing says:
"In the desire realm, form is coarse."
The great elements of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are infused within the body,
like water entering sand;
they do not occupy a different location because their nature is distinct.
Therefore, it is not the case that they occupy the same location yet are not inseparable.
That refers to the meaning of being either separate or inseparable.

However, the concepts of separation and non-separation generally concern matter that shares the same stage (*bhūmi*), persists from beginning to end, exists within the same aggregate (*saṃghāta*), and is nourished by maturation (*vipāka*) and sustenance (*āhāra*).
Because this matter bound to the upper realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*) abides within a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
it does not have the sense of being either separated or inseparable from it. Ce says:
When the forms of the desire realm and the form realm coexist within a single body without mutual obstruction,
this is termed "intermingling."
